domains.description: A timed, mixed-branch final assessment simulating exam conditions: no hints, strict time limits, questions drawn from every domain. Take it mid-course as a diagnostic and again at the end.

domains.name: Medieval Philosophy
domains.summary: Faith seeking understanding: Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, the Islamic Golden Age of Avicenna and Averroes, and Ockham's razor.

scenarios.title: The Privation Defense
scenarios.situation: A skeptic asks Augustine: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why does evil exist? Did God create evil?'
choices: Redefine the explanandum: evil is not a created thing but privation — the corruption or absence of good in a thing. God created good things with the capacity to be corrupted; the corruption itself is not a substance God made. The question 'who created evil?' presupposes evil is a thing.
Deny that evil exists — suffering is an illusion.
Say God is not all-powerful.
Blame human free will exclusively, with no metaphysical account.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B (index 1). Augustine's privation theory answers the metaphysical question (what is evil?) before the moral one (why permit it?): evil as corruption presupposes a good nature corrupted — blindness presupposes sight. This dissolves the Manichean picture of evil as a rival cosmic substance, which would make the problem of evil insoluble. The free-will defense then addresses permission: rational creatures can misuse their good will. Two questions, two answers — conflating them is the classic error.
scenarios.hint: Is the skeptic's question ('who created evil?') well-formed on Augustine's view?
evidence: Evil = absence/corruption of good, not a substance; dissolves Manichean dualism.

scenarios.title: The Fool's Concept
scenarios.situation: Anselm argues from the fool's own concept: even the atheist understands 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' — and a God existing only in the mind is less great than one existing in reality too.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the argument most vulnerable?
choices: The conclusion — it proves too little.
It has no vulnerability; it is airtight.

Premise 3 — that existence in reality is a 'greatness-making' property. Kant's objection ('existence is not a predicate') denies that existing adds to a concept's greatness: a hundred real thalers contain no more coins than a hundred possible thalers. If existence is not a perfection, the inference collapses.
Premise 1 — atheists have no concept of God.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The argument's engine is the claim that real existence makes a being greater — without it, the fool can grant the concept and deny the reality with no contradiction. Kant's critique targets exactly this: existence is not a property that enriches a concept but the positing of the concept's object. Defenders reply that necessary existence (not mere existence) is the perfection — shifting the argument to modal versions (Hartshorne, Plantinga). The debate's movement is the lesson: each repair relocates the pressure point.
scenarios.hint: Does adding 'exists' to a concept make the concept greater?
evidence: Tries to derive existence from definition; pressure point = existence as perfection.

scenarios.title: The Contingency Way
scenarios.situation: Aquinas's Third Way: contingent things exist; if everything were contingent, once nothing existed; from nothing, nothing comes; so something necessary exists.
scenarios.prompt: Which step would a naturalist most plausibly challenge?
choices: That contingent things exist — obviously false.
That nothing comes from nothing — obviously false.
The conclusion names God — names prove nothing.

The 'once nothing existed' step: from 'each thing is contingent' it does not follow that 'there was a time when everything was non-existent' — an infinite series of contingent beings, each caused by an earlier one, is not ruled out by the premises. The quantifier shift (each-contingent vs all-contingent-at-once) is the gap.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The Third Way moves from the contingency of each thing to the contingency of the whole series — a quantifier-shift fallacy unless defended. The naturalist can grant every being is contingent while insisting the series itself is beginningless: each member explained by its predecessor, no first member needed. Aquinas needs the further premise that an essentially (not merely temporally) ordered series requires a first — which is where the real debate lives, in the First Way's machinery.
scenarios.hint: Does 'every member is contingent' entail 'the series might all have failed at once'?
evidence: From contingency to necessary being; vulnerable at the quantifier shift.

scenarios.title: The Man Who Cannot Feel
scenarios.situation: Avicenna asks us to imagine a man created fully formed, suspended in air, senses veiled — no sight, no touch, no body awareness. He would still know that he exists.
scenarios.prompt: What does the thought experiment argue?
choices: That self-awareness is direct and non-bodily: knowledge of one's own existence does not go through the senses or body awareness, so the soul (the self) is distinct from the body — a substance known without any material intermediary.
That floating is the natural state of the soul.
That the senses are useless.
That Avicenna believed in levitation.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The flying man isolates the variable: subtract every bodily sensation and self-knowledge remains — so self-knowledge does not depend on the body. It is a dualist argument from epistemology: what is known without the body is distinct from the body. Descartes' cogito runs the same move seven centuries later (doubt everything bodily; the thinking self survives). The experiment's power is its minimalism: no theology, just first-person certainty under sensory deprivation.
scenarios.hint: What survives when every bodily sensation is subtracted?
evidence: Self-awareness without body awareness; epistemological argument for soul's distinctness.

scenarios.title: Two Truths?
scenarios.situation: Scripture seems to say the world had a beginning; philosophy demonstrates it is eternal. Averroes denies there are 'two truths.'
choices: Reason always loses to authority.

Truth is one: where demonstration conflicts with the literal text, the text must be read allegorically — reason determines the correct interpretation. Philosophy does not contradict revelation; it corrects our reading of it. There cannot be two truths because truth does not contradict itself.
Philosophy is true for philosophers, religion true for the masses — double truth.
Scripture always wins over reason.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Averroes's 'double truth' is a misattribution by his critics: his actual position is the unity of truth with reason as the interpreter. When demonstration is certain and the text seems to disagree, the literal reading must yield — not because reason outranks revelation, but because God cannot contradict Himself, so the intended meaning must be non-literal. This made him radical: it gives philosophers authority over scriptural interpretation, which is why theologians attacked him.
scenarios.hint: If truth is one, who decides what the text means when demonstration disagrees?
evidence: Truth is one; reason interprets scripture allegorically where demonstration conflicts.

scenarios.title: Shaving Universals
scenarios.situation: The realist says 'humanity' is a real universal shared by all humans, explaining their resemblance. Ockham reaches for his razor.
scenarios.prompt: What does the razor cut, and why?
choices: The concept 'humanity' — we should stop using the word.
Nothing; the razor only applies to physics.

The universal-entity: resembling particular humans plus the mind's concept of them explains everything the universal was meant to explain, so the extra entity does no work. The razor is not 'simpler is truer' but 'do not posit entities that earn no explanatory keep.'
Human beings — Ockham was a misanthrope.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Ockham's nominalism: only particulars exist; universals are names/concepts. The razor justifies the cut methodologically: if the concept does the explaining, the metaphysical entity is redundant. Note what survives: resemblance (real), concepts (real as mental acts), language (useful). What goes is the shared entity. The move generalizes: every abstract entity in your ontology must pay explanatory rent or face the blade.
scenarios.hint: What explanatory work did the universal do that the concept cannot?
evidence: Do not multiply entities beyond necessity; universals shaved to concepts.

scenarios.title: The Unjust Law
scenarios.situation: Aquinas says an unjust law is 'no law at all' but a 'violence.' A tyrant's enforcer replies: 'It was properly enacted — it IS law.'
choices: That unjust laws should always be violently resisted.
That no law is ever valid.
That 'unjust law' is a contradiction, so injustice cannot exist.

That law's nature includes orientation to the common good and consistency with natural law: a gravely unjust enactment fails as law the way a fake knife fails as a knife — it has the shape but not the function. This does not license anarchy: Aquinas counsels obedience to tolerable injustice for order's sake, resisting only grave cases.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Aquinas's claim is about law's focal meaning: law is essentially an ordinance of reason for the common good, so extreme injustice makes an enactment law only in a secondary, defective sense. But he is no revolutionary: he distinguishes the metaphysical point (it fails as law) from the practical counsel (obey unless it commands sin or gravely violates justice, since disorder is itself an evil). The position threads natural-law morality through political prudence.
scenarios.hint: Does 'no law at all' mean 'disobey every flawed statute'?
evidence: Gravely unjust enactment fails as law; obedience still counseled short of grave cases.

domains.name: Modern Philosophy
domains.summary: From Descartes' doubt through rationalists and empiricists to Kant's Copernican turn — and beyond to Hegel and Nietzsche.

scenarios.title: The Demon-Proof Belief
scenarios.situation: Descartes imagines an evil demon deceiving him about everything — the sky, his body, mathematics itself. One belief survives.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the cogito survive the demon?
choices: Because Descartes simply asserts it without argument.
It does not survive; the demon defeats it too.

Because deception presupposes a subject: the demon can fake the world but cannot fake there being someone to deceive. 'I am deceived' entails 'I exist' — the attempt to doubt one's existence performs the existence it doubts.
Because the demon is not powerful enough to touch the soul.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The cogito's immunity is performative: doubting is a kind of thinking, and thinking requires a thinker. The demon can corrupt every content of thought but not the existence of the thinking — 'I think' is self-verifying in the act of entertaining it. Note the modesty: what survives is the thinking thing's existence, not its nature — the 'I' here is thin, and the rebuild (body, world, God) is the Meditations' remaining work.
scenarios.hint: What must exist for deception to occur?
evidence: 'I think, therefore I am': doubting presupposes the doubter; demon-proof.

scenarios.title: One Substance
scenarios.situation: Spinoza argues there can only be one substance. A critic says: 'But I see many things — tables, people, stars.'
choices: That tables and people are illusions.
That he only meant one substance per attribute.
He cannot reply; the objection is fatal.

That tables and people are modes — ways the one substance is modified — not substances themselves. Plurality exists at the level of modes; unity at the level of substance. The critic confuses being a thing with being a substance (what exists in itself).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Spinoza's ontology has two levels: substance (what is in itself, conceived through itself — exactly one) and modes (what is in another — everything finite). Your body is a mode of extension; your mind a mode of thought; both are the one substance under different attributes. The system thus accommodates all observed plurality while denying it substantial independence — like waves are many but the sea is one.
scenarios.hint: Is a wave a separate thing from the sea, or a way the sea is?
evidence: One substance (God-or-Nature); finite things are its modes, not substances.

scenarios.title: Why This?
scenarios.situation: Leibniz's Principle of Sufficient Reason: for everything, there is a reason why it is so rather than otherwise. A critic asks: 'What is the reason for the universe as a whole?'
choices: To a necessary being outside the series of contingent things: every contingent thing's reason lies in another, but the whole series' reason cannot lie within it (that would be circular) — so it lies in a being whose reason is in itself, existing necessarily. The PSR becomes a cosmological argument.
Nowhere — the question is meaningless.
To an infinite regress, which Leibniz accepts.
To the conclusion that the universe has no reason.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Leibniz's move (in 'On the Ultimate Origination of Things'): the PSR demands a reason for the entire contingent series, and since no member can ground the whole, the ground must be extramundane — a necessary being carrying its reason within itself. Critics attack the PSR itself (why must the whole have a reason? — a composition-fallacy charge) or accept brute contingency. The debate is about how far explanation must go: PSR says all the way down; its deniers say explanation can stop.
scenarios.hint: Can the reason for the whole series be one of its members?
evidence: Everything has a reason; applied to the whole series yields a necessary being.

scenarios.title: The Unperceived Tree
scenarios.situation: 'If a tree falls in a forest with no one around, does Berkeley say it makes a sound — or exists at all?'
choices: That matter sustains the tree — Berkeley was a materialist.

That the tree exists as an idea in God's mind: esse est percipi applies to finite minds, but God perceives all — so unperceived-by-us things still exist, sustained by divine perception. Continuity is guaranteed theologically, not materially.
That the tree pops out of existence when unobserved.
That the question is meaningless.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Berkeley is routinely caricatured as saying things blink out when unobserved; his actual view invokes God as the universal perceiver, guaranteeing the order and continuity of ideas. Matter — mind-independent stuff — is what he denies, as an empty abstraction doing no work: all we ever encounter are ideas, so positing matter behind them violates (proto-)Ockham. Whether the God-move is ad hoc or elegant is the standard exam question.
scenarios.hint: Who perceives the tree when no finite mind does?
evidence: To be is to be perceived; unperceived things sustained by God's perception.

scenarios.title: The Wise Proportion
scenarios.situation: Hume argues a wise person proportions belief to evidence, and that no testimony suffices to establish a miracle.
choices: That witnesses always lie.
That religion is false.

That uniform experience against miracles constitutes a full proof, while testimony's reliability is merely probable — so the stronger evidence (uniform experience) always outweighs the weaker (testimony). Belief should follow the weight, not the wonder.
That miracles are logically impossible.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Hume's 'Of Miracles' is an evidence-weighing argument, not a metaphysical ban: a miracle is by definition a violation of laws established by uniform experience — the strongest possible empirical evidence. Testimony, however sincere, is weaker evidence (witnesses err, lie, love wonder). So the rational credence never reaches 'miracle occurred.' Critics reply that uniform experience begs the question (it assumes the very closed system at issue) — the live debate is about prior probabilities, not testimony per se.
scenarios.hint: Which is stronger evidence: uniform experience or human testimony?
evidence: Uniform experience outweighs testimony; wise belief proportions to evidence.

scenarios.situation: Kant claims '7 + 5 = 12' is synthetic a priori: informative (the concept '12' is not contained in '7 + 5') yet known without experience.
choices: It is just a math fact with no philosophical import.
Because Kant was bad at arithmetic.
It proves empiricism true.

Because it is Kant's answer to Hume: if some informative truths are knowable a priori, then necessity in science need not come from experience — it comes from the mind's own forms (here, the pure intuition of time as successive synthesis). The synthetic a priori is the hinge of the whole critical system.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The synthetic a priori is Kant's master category: Hume showed matters of fact lack necessity; rationalists bought necessity at the price of emptiness (analytic). Kant's third option — informative yet necessary, grounded in the mind's forms — rescues causality, mathematics, and science's necessity in one move. Attack the example (is arithmetic really synthetic? Frege and later logicians said no) and the system's hinge creaks — which is why the example is endlessly contested.
scenarios.hint: If arithmetic is synthetic a priori, where does its necessity come from?
evidence: Informative yet knowable without experience; Kant's answer to Hume.

scenarios.title: God Is Dead
scenarios.situation: Nietzsche's madman announces 'God is dead.' A student reads this as atheist celebration.
choices: That the event is a catastrophe, not a triumph: the Christian-Platonic value system that gave life meaning has collapsed under its own intellectual honesty, and nothing yet replaces it — nihilism is the danger to overcome, not the goal. The madman mourns; the revaluation of values is the unfinished task.
That atheism has won and we should celebrate.
That God literally died at a specific date.
That Nietzsche was a nihilist.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'God is dead' describes a cultural event — the undermining of the highest values' credibility — and the madman asks 'who will wipe this blood off us?' The death of God is the problem to which the Übermensch and revaluation are proposed solutions. Reading Nietzsche as a cheerful nihilist inverts him: he is nihilism's physician, diagnosing the disease (value-collapse) to prescribe the cure (creating values from strength, amor fati).
scenarios.hint: Does the madman celebrate or mourn?
evidence: Collapse of the value system; nihilism as danger to overcome, not goal.

domains.name: Ethics
domains.summary: What is right? Metaethics, utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics, and hard applied cases.

scenarios.title: Divert or Push?
scenarios.situation: A runaway trolley will kill five. You can divert it to kill one (lever case), or push a large person off a bridge to stop it (push case). Most people judge diverting permissible and pushing wrong — though the numbers are identical.
choices: Whether trolleys are dangerous.
Whether you are brave enough to push.
There is no question; the numbers settle it.

What explains the verdict difference? Candidate explanations: the doctrine of double effect (intended vs foreseen killing), agent-centered constraints (using as mere means), or the personal-force hypothesis. The puzzle is not 'which would you do?' but which principle accounts for the stable intuition pattern.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The trolley problem is a diagnostic instrument: the lever/push asymmetry is data, and rival moral theories compete to explain it. Consequentialists must explain why pushing feels wrong (or debunk the feeling); deontologists cite the means/end distinction; Thomson herself used variants to test the explanations. Students who answer with their gut verdict miss the point — the exam asks for the explanatory principle and its costs.
scenarios.hint: What would a good explanation of the asymmetry look like?
evidence: Lever/push asymmetry as data; competing explanations (double effect, means/ends).

scenarios.title: The Competent Judge
scenarios.situation: Mill says higher pleasures outweigh lower ones, judged by 'competent judges' who have experienced both. A critic says this is elitist: who are these judges, and why trust them?
choices: That the judges' preference is evidence, not authority: those who know both kinds of pleasure systematically prefer the higher — and their preference needs no further credential, just as we trust tasters about wine. The charge of elitism confuses expertise with class; the test is experience, open in principle to all.
That only aristocrats count as judges.
That lower pleasures do not matter at all.
He cannot reply; elitism refutes him.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mill's move is empirical: ask people who know both, and they prefer Socrates dissatisfied to the fool satisfied — even while sometimes choosing the lower (weakness of will explains the gap). The 'competent judge' is anyone with the relevant experience, not a social rank. Whether the preference data actually supports Mill (do the experienced really prefer the higher?) is the live empirical question — and the exam's follow-up.
scenarios.hint: Is Mill appealing to authority or to evidence?
evidence: Competent judges' preference as evidence; experience, not rank, qualifies.

scenarios.title: Lying to the Murderer
scenarios.situation: A murderer at the door asks where your friend is hiding. Kant's strict view: do not lie — even here.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest Kantian defense?
choices: There is no defense; Kant was wrong.

That the duty not to lie protects the shared condition of rational agency — truth-telling as such; making exceptions for consequences reintroduces consequentialism through the back door, and you cannot control the consequences anyway (the friend may have slipped out; your lie may cause the harm). Responsibility tracks your maxim, not outcomes.
That lying is always easy to detect.
That the murderer will not believe you.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Kant's defense has two strands: principled (exceptions destroy the universality that gives the duty its authority — a 'no lying except when useful' maxim is just consequentialism) and epistemic (you cannot know the lie helps; the friend may have escaped, and then your lie sends the murderer after them). Modern Kantians add the third option: refuse to answer, or mislead without lying — though critics ask whether that distinction survives scrutiny.
scenarios.hint: If you may lie whenever it helps, what remains of the duty not to lie?
evidence: Kant: no lying even here; duty protects truth-telling as such.

scenarios.title: The Two Drivers
scenarios.situation: Two equally reckless drivers run a red light. One hits no one; the other kills a child. Our blame differs enormously — though their agency was identical.
scenarios.prompt: What is the problem of moral luck?
choices: That luck does not exist.
There is no problem; blame tracks outcomes, fairly.

That moral assessment depends on factors beyond the agent's control (constitutive, circumstantial, resultant luck) — yet morality seems to require control. Nagel's paradox: we condemn the killer-driver more, but the difference (a pedestrian's presence) was luck, not agency. Either luck infects morality or our blame practices are irrational.
That reckless driving is legal.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (Nagel, Williams). Resultant luck: outcomes beyond control affect blame. Circumstantial luck: the situations we face are luck. Constitutive luck: our very character is luck. Together they threaten the control condition on responsibility — the Kantian core that morality must be about what is up to us. Responses: restrict blame to the will (Kantian), accept luck's role (revise the control condition), or distinguish blame from moral assessment. The paradox structures the whole debate.
scenarios.hint: What did the killer-driver control that the lucky one did not?
evidence: Blame depends on luck (resultant, circumstantial, constitutive); threatens control condition.

scenarios.title: How Much Must You Give?
scenarios.situation: Singer argues: if you can prevent suffering at modest cost, you must — the drowning child in the pond generalizes to global poverty. Taken seriously, this demands giving away most of your income.
choices: That charity is inefficient.
That the drowning child analogy fails because ponds are rare.
There is no objection; everyone agrees.

That a moral theory requiring near-total self-sacrifice is too demanding to be true — it alienates agents from their own lives (Williams: it attacks integrity, the projects that make a life one's own). Either the theory is false or 'ought' does not imply what we thought. Singer's reply: the objection confuses what is true with what is comfortable.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The demandingness objection (Williams, Scheffler) targets consequentialism's core: impartial maximization leaves no room for the agent's own projects, relationships, and partiality — the things that make a life worth living. If morality demands sainthood, something is wrong with the theory (or with our conception of morality's stringency). Singer bites the bullet: our comfort with moderate giving is moral complacency, not a philosophical objection. The standoff is genuine.
scenarios.hint: Can a true moral theory demand you abandon everything that makes your life yours?
evidence: Must morality permit personal projects, or demand impartial maximization?

scenarios.title: The Error Theorist's Life
scenarios.situation: Mackie's error theory says all moral claims are false (they presuppose nonexistent moral facts). A critic asks: 'So you think torturing children is... not wrong?'
scenarios.prompt: How does the error theorist reply?
choices: By abandoning error theory.
By saying 'wrong' is meaningless noise.

By distinguishing levels: 'torturing children is wrong' is false strictly (no moral facts), but the error theorist can still condemn torture — as an expression of attitude, or via a fictionalist 'as if' morality. The question confuses the metaethical claim (about facts) with the first-order stance (about torture).
By agreeing that torture is fine.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). The error theorist's standard move is a two-level response: at the meta level, moral discourse is systematically false (like witch discourse); at the practical level, we keep the discourse — via fictionalism (act as if), expressivism about our own commitments, or revolutionary reform. The critic's 'gotcha' assumes error theory must change first-order behavior; it need not. Whether the two levels can stably coexist (can you condemn what you believe is strictly false?) is the real pressure point.
scenarios.hint: Does denying moral facts require approving of torture?
evidence: All moral claims false (no moral facts); practice continues via fictionalism/attitude.

scenarios.title: The Species Boundary
scenarios.situation: Singer argues that excluding animals from moral consideration because of species membership is 'speciesism' — like racism, an arbitrary boundary.
choices: That we should never use animals for anything.

An argument from marginal cases plus sentience: if the morally relevant feature is suffering, then species is irrelevant — what matters is sentience, which many animals share. Any boundary that includes all humans but excludes sentient animals must cite a feature beyond species, or stand condemned as arbitrary.
That animals are exactly like humans.
That species do not exist biologically.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The argument: (1) suffering is what matters morally; (2) many non-humans suffer; (3) species membership is morally irrelevant (like race); therefore (4) animal suffering counts. The 'marginal cases' reinforce: any capacity-based cutoff (reason, language) that excludes animals also excludes some humans — so defenders of the boundary must either accept that or find another feature. Replies: Cohen (rights need moral agency), or species-membership as morally relevant in itself. The structure, not the diet, is the exam point.
scenarios.hint: What morally relevant feature distinguishes all humans from all sentient animals?
evidence: Sentience, not species, is the morally relevant boundary; marginal-cases argument.

domains.name: Epistemology
domains.summary: What is knowledge? Justified true belief and Gettier, skepticism, rationalism vs empiricism, reliabilism, testimony and disagreement.

scenarios.title: The Lucky Promotion
scenarios.situation: You believe your colleague got the promotion because the manager told you so and you saw her name on the draft announcement. In fact the manager was misinformed and the draft was outdated — but by coincidence, your colleague DID get the promotion (decided later, for other reasons).
scenarios.prompt: Do you know she got the promotion?
choices: No — this is a Gettier case: your belief is true and justified, but the justification is disconnected from the truth (it pointed at misinformation and a stale draft). Knowledge requires the truth to be non-accidentally connected to your reasons, not merely coincident with them.
Yes — true belief with good reasons is knowledge.
Yes — the outcome is what matters.
No — because managers always lie.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The structure mirrors Gettier's originals: justification (manager's word, draft) + truth (she was promoted) + disconnect (the promotion happened for unrelated reasons, later). The belief is lucky-true. This is why post-Gettier epistemology adds conditions like sensitivity, safety, or aptness (Sosa): the belief must be true BECAUSE of the agent's competence, not alongside it. In tech terms: your monitor was broken but happened to show the right number — that is not monitoring.
scenarios.hint: Would you still 'know' if the coincidence had gone the other way?
evidence: Justified true belief by luck is not knowledge; truth must connect to justification.

scenarios.title: Hands and Vats
scenarios.situation: You claim to know you have hands. The skeptic notes: 'I have hands' entails 'I am not a handless brain in a vat.' You admit you cannot rule out the vat scenario.
scenarios.prompt: What follows, by the skeptic's logic?
choices: That you should stop claiming things.

By closure: if you know P ('I have hands') and know P entails Q ('I am not a handless vat-brain'), you know Q. You concede you do not know Q — so, by modus tollens on closure, you do not know P. The skeptic's engine is closure plus indistinguishability.
Nothing — closure is obviously false.
That brains in vats cannot have hands.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The argument's validity is not in question — it is a clean modus tollens on the closure principle. The fight is over the premises: deny P1 (contextualism: in ordinary contexts you DO know you are not a vat-brain; the skeptic illicitly raises the standards), deny closure (Dretske/Nozick: knowledge does not always transmit across known entailment), or go Moorean (your knowledge of hands is better evidence than any skeptical premise). Each denial is a theory of knowledge. Pick your poison — but pick knowingly.
scenarios.hint: Which premise would you deny, and what theory does that denial commit you to?
evidence: Knowing P + P entails Q -> knowing Q; skeptic's engine with vat scenarios.

scenarios.title: The Reliable Thermometer
scenarios.situation: Your building's thermometer is perfectly reliable, and you form beliefs about the temperature by reading it — but you have no idea whether it is reliable; for all you know it is broken.
scenarios.prompt: Are your temperature beliefs justified, on reliabilism?
choices: No — thermometers cannot justify beliefs.
Yes — because you feel confident.

Yes — reliabilism makes justification external: what matters is the process's actual reliability, not your beliefs about it. The thermometer is reliable, so the beliefs are justified, even though you cannot cite the reliability from the inside. This externalism is reliabilism's feature and its scandal.
No — justification requires knowing your sources are reliable.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Process reliabilism (Goldman) severs justification from the agent's perspective: a belief is justified iff produced by a reliable process, full stop. The thermometer-reader is the poster case — and the new-evil-demon problem is the mirror: a victim with identical experiences but an unreliable world seems justified yet counts as unjustified. The internalism/externalism fault line runs exactly here: is justification about your perspective or the world's cooperation?
scenarios.hint: Should justification depend on facts you cannot access?
evidence: Justification = reliable process; external — your perspective is not required.

scenarios.title: The Split Bill
scenarios.situation: You and a friend — both excellent at mental arithmetic — split a restaurant bill. You calculate $43, she calculates $45. You have no reason to think yourself more reliable.
choices: Insist on $43 — you did the math.
Insist on $45 — politeness demands it.
Order dessert to change the subject.

Lower your confidence substantially: with an epistemic peer, same evidence, and no asymmetry, sticking to $43 is arbitrary — you should suspend judgment or split the difference. Your original reasoning is now just one of two equally good data points.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Conciliationism (Christensen, Elga): peer disagreement is higher-order evidence that you may have erred, and rationality requires updating on it. The restaurant case is deliberately clean — no ego, no expertise gap — to isolate the principle. The controversy is the scale-up: applied to philosophy or politics, conciliationism seems to mandate skepticism about most contested beliefs. Steadfasters reply that your reasoning is private evidence the peer lacks. The exam question is always the scale-up.
scenarios.hint: Is your calculation now one data point or the only data point?
evidence: Peer disagreement is evidence you erred; adjust confidence accordingly.

scenarios.title: The Child and the Expert
scenarios.situation: A child believes the earth is round because her teacher said so. A physicist believes it because of the evidence. Both beliefs are true.
scenarios.prompt: What does the testimony debate ask about the child's belief?
choices: Whether testimony alone — without independent verification — can yield knowledge (non-reductionism: yes, we are entitled to trust by default) or whether it needs its own backing (reductionism: the child needs reasons to trust the teacher). The physicist's case is easy; the child's is the test.
Whether children should be in school.
Whether the earth is actually round.
Nothing — testimony never yields knowledge.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Nearly all our knowledge rides on testimony — you have not personally verified most of what you know. Reductionists (Hume) demand that testimony be backed by induction over past reliability; non-reductionists (Reid, Burge) treat trust as a default entitlement, defeated only by contrary evidence. The child's case isolates the question: she has no track record of the teacher's reliability, yet we want to say she knows. If reductionism cannot accommodate her, so much the worse for reductionism.
scenarios.hint: Have you personally verified most of what you claim to know?
evidence: Does testimony need independent backing, or is trust the default?

scenarios.title: The Turkey's Science
scenarios.situation: A turkey observes 364 days of feeding at 9 AM and infers day 365 will bring food. Day 365 is Thanksgiving. (Russell's chicken.)
scenarios.prompt: What does the case show about induction?
choices: That Thanksgiving refutes science.

That enumerative induction has no rational foundation: the inference 'observed regularities continue' itself assumes the uniformity of nature — which is what needed proving. Hume's point is not that induction fails (it works) but that reason cannot vindicate it; custom carries the weight.
That turkeys are bad statisticians.
That induction is logically valid.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Russell's turkey dramatizes Hume's problem: every justification of induction either deduces (impossible — the future might differ) or induces (circular — assuming uniformity to prove uniformity). The turkey's reasoning was impeccable by inductivist lights and catastrophically wrong. Responses: pragmatic vindication (Reichenbach: if anything works, induction does), dissolution (Goodman: the problem is which regularities to project — grue), or acceptance (Hume: custom, not reason, is our nature).
scenarios.hint: What justifies expecting the future to resemble the past — without assuming it?
evidence: No non-circular rational justification; custom, not reason, grounds it.

scenarios.title: The Lottery Paradox
scenarios.situation: A fair lottery has 1,000,000 tickets. For each ticket, the probability it loses is 0.999999 — high enough, it seems, to justify believing 'ticket 1 loses,' 'ticket 2 loses,' ... Yet you also justifiably believe 'some ticket wins.' Contradiction.
choices: That lotteries are unfair.
That probability is useless.
Nothing — paradoxes are just puzzles.

High-probability accounts of justification: if 0.999999 suffices for justified belief in each 'loses' claim, closure (or agglomeration) yields justified belief in their conjunction — which contradicts the justified belief that some ticket wins. Something must give: the threshold, closure, or the link between probability and belief.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). The lottery paradox (Kyburg) is a stress test for fallibilism: we want both (a) high probability to justify belief and (b) consistency of our justified beliefs, but the lottery shows they conflict under closure. Live options: deny the threshold justifies (knowledge needs more than probability — safety, normic support), deny agglomeration (Smith), or accept inconsistency (paraconsistent). The paradox matters because real beliefs — 'my flight will land,' 'this code is correct' — are all merely probable.
scenarios.hint: Can you justifiably believe each ticket loses AND that some ticket wins?
evidence: High probability per-ticket vs consistency; threatens probabilistic justification.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Core concepts
concepts: Logic is the study of good inference. Deduction preserves truth: a valid argument's conclusion must follow if the premises are true. Soundness adds true premises. Most real-world bad arguments are valid-but-unsound — perfect machinery fed false fuel — so auditing premises matters more than admiring form.

Epistemology asks what knowledge is and when we have it. The classic analysis — justified true belief — was shaken by Gettier (1963): luckily-true beliefs with broken justification are not knowledge. For technical work, the moral is operational: a true finding from a broken instrument is not a finding.

Ethics offers competing standards: utilitarianism judges by consequences (maximize well-being), deontology by duties (some acts are forbidden regardless of payoff), virtue ethics by character (what would the excellent practitioner do?). Applied ethics is largely the disciplined negotiation among these three.

Philosophy of mind interrogates claims about understanding and consciousness. Searle's Chinese room (1980) argues syntax is not semantics: perfect symbol-manipulation need not be understanding. Functionalism counters that the right functional organization is what matters. The debate sets the terms for every 'does the AI understand?' dispute.

Political philosophy supplies design devices: Rawls' veil of ignorance forces rules justifiable from every position in the system, filtering self-serving policy. It is a practical tool for AI governance, not just a classroom puzzle.

Hume's is-ought gap guards the border between description and prescription: no 'is' entails an 'ought' without a value premise. 'The data shows X' never by itself yields 'we must do Y' — the missing premise is where the real argument lives.

example.code:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# Truth-table check: is modus ponens valid?
print("P Q | (P->Q), P |- Q")
for P in (True, False):
    for Q in (True, False):
        imp = (not P) or Q
        # argument valid iff no row has true premises and false conclusion
        bad = imp and P and not Q
        print(P, Q, "|", imp, P, "->", (not bad and (imp and P) <= Q), "bad-row:", bad)
print("No bad rows: the form is valid regardless of what P and Q mean.")
EOF
example.walkthrough: The truth table tests form, not content: there is no row where the premises are true and the conclusion false, so modus ponens is valid for any P and Q. Validity is a property of structure — which is exactly why it cannot rescue false premises.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling an argument 'invalid' when you mean 'unsound' — if the conclusion follows from the premises, the logic is fine and the premises are the problem.
Common trap: treating thought experiments as empirical evidence — the Chinese room and the veil of ignorance isolate concepts; they prove distinctions, not facts about brains or policies.
Common trap: letting 'the data says' smuggle values — every is-to-ought inference hides a normative premise; find it before obeying the conclusion.
Common trap: assuming frameworks must be chosen exclusively — real ethical reasoning often layers them: duties as constraints, utility within constraints, virtue as the practitioner's aim.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Philosophy move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Philosophy
concepts: Philosophy is a multi-step process within Philosophy: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Philosophy to the broader Philosophy ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Philosophy begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Philosophy. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Philosophy as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Philosophy flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp is organized as domains (major areas). Each domain holds lessons (concept briefings), scenarios (graded thought experiments and argument analyses), and labs (hands-on exercises like argument maps and essay outlines).
The intended loop is: read a lesson, attempt its scenarios closed-book, then do the lab. Passive reading alone does not build philosophical skill — reconstruction does.
Scenarios are multiple-choice but scored like arguments: every wrong choice names a real fallacy or confusion, and the explanation teaches the distinction you missed.
The mock-assessment domain is a timed final; the capstone-build domain guides you to write a defended 1,500-word position paper across the course.

example.code:
A 60-minute study block:
  0:00-0:15  re-read the lesson, marking each argument's premises
  0:15-0:40  scenarios closed-book, committing to an answer first
  0:40-0:55  lab (argument map or outline)
  0:55-1:00  error log: one line per miss
example.walkthrough: One focused hour beats three distracted ones. The final five minutes — the error log — is where the learning compounds, because it converts each miss into a revisit target.

pitfalls: Reading lessons like articles: highlighting nothing, testing nothing, reconstructing nothing.
Peeking at the answer before committing to a choice — the commitment is the training.
Skipping labs because 'I understood it.' Recognition is not production; write the argument out.
lessons.try_it: Run the 4 orientation scenarios in this domain closed-book, then begin Ancient Philosophy.

lessons.title: Your Study Strategy: Argument-First Learning
concepts: Philosophy exams reward reconstructing arguments, not reciting names. For every thinker, learn the premises, the inference, and the conclusion — the 'because' chain that earns the conclusion.

Steelman before you criticize: restate a view so well its defender would accept your version. This is also how you earn full marks on 'evaluate' questions — examiners reward the strongest objection, not the cheapest.
Interleave branches: study ethics and epistemology in the same week. Mixed practice forces you to select the right toolkit, and selection under pressure is the exam skill.
Keep an objection ledger: every time a scenario fools you, write the confused distinction in one line and revisit it weekly until it stops fooling you.

example.code:
Objection-ledger entry format:
  CONFUSED: validity vs soundness
  FIX: validity = form (conclusion must follow); soundness = valid + true premises
  REVISIT: Sunday
example.walkthrough: The ledger turns each mistake into a future point. Students who maintain one consistently outperform re-readers, because re-reading rehearses what you already know.

pitfalls: Memorizing conclusions without the argument that earns them — conclusions are cheap, arguments are the currency.
Studying one branch for weeks. The exam mixes branches; your practice should too.
Confusing familiarity ('I've seen this') with mastery ('I can reconstruct it cold').
lessons.try_it: Start your objection ledger today with one entry from the orientation scenarios.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: The Thirteen Domains
concepts: History arc: Ancient (Presocratics through Aristotle to the Hellenistic schools), Medieval (Augustine, Aquinas, the Islamic Golden Age), Modern (Descartes through Kant). Each era answers the previous era's failures — the replies only make sense in order.

Systematic branches: Ethics (what is right), Epistemology (what is known), Metaphysics (what is real), Logic (what follows), Philosophy of Mind (what thinking is), Political Philosophy (what is just).
Skills arc: start-here (orientation) gives way to ten content domains, then mock-assessment (a timed trial under exam conditions), then capstone-build (your defended thesis).
The phil-exam-prep domain collects strategy: essay structure, command words, the highest-yield distinctions, and a final-week revision protocol.

example.code:
Roadmap:
  start-here -> ancient -> medieval -> modern
      -> ethics | epistemology | metaphysics | logic | mind | political
      -> mock-assessment -> capstone-build
  (phil-exam-prep runs alongside the final third)
example.walkthrough: Follow the history arc first. Later thinkers constantly reply to earlier ones — Hume replies to Locke, Kant replies to Hume — and without the original move, the reply is noise.

pitfalls: Jumping to modern philosophy without the ancient background it reacts to.
Treating the branches as isolated silos. Exam questions cross them deliberately.
Saving the mock assessment for 'when ready.' Take it early as a diagnostic; readiness follows measurement.
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list, mark the two branches you know least, and schedule them first.

lessons.title: Labs, Scenarios, and the Mock Assessment
concepts: Labs are structured analysis exercises: argument maps, essay outlines, distinction drills. Their 'checks' are self-verification prompts — distinctive phrases your work should contain — not auto-graders.
Scenarios carry metadata: objectives (what is tested), mins (budget your time like an exam), evidence (the reference fact), and a hint. Use the hint only after committing to an answer.
The mock assessment simulates exam pressure: mixed-branch questions, no hints, strict time. Take it twice — once mid-course as a diagnostic, once at the end.
The capstone asks for a 1,500-word defended position paper: thesis, exposition, steelmanned opposition, replies, conclusion. It is the single best exam-prep artifact you can produce.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  90 minutes, no notes, branches mixed
  -> score -> log every miss in the objection ledger
  -> re-study only the missed distinctions, not everything
example.walkthrough: Two timed runs typically lift scores more than a week of re-reading, because they train retrieval and selection under pressure — the actual exam conditions.

pitfalls: Using hints as a first resort instead of a last one.
Treating the capstone as optional. It is the highest-ROI domain in the course.
Reviewing only correct answers. The misses are the curriculum.
lessons.try_it: Do one lab from the Logic domain today to feel the format before you need it under pressure.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 1 — Choose and Frame Your Thesis
concepts: A good thesis is contestable, narrow, and arguable in 1,500 words: 'Utilitarianism is the best framework for AI policy' beats 'Ethics is important.' Narrowness is what makes depth possible.
Frame it as a because-claim: 'X because [reason 1] and [reason 2].' If you cannot state the 'because' in one sentence, the thesis is not ready.
Pick a thesis where you can name the strongest opposition in advance. If you cannot imagine who disagrees and why, you have picked a slogan, not a thesis.
Write a 200-word prospectus first: thesis, two supporting arguments sketched, the strongest objection named. Get the shape right before drafting.

example.code:
Prospectus template:
  THESIS: Autonomous-vehicle policy should be deontological, not utilitarian,
           because aggregate-benefit calculations license sacrificing identifiable
           individuals, violating a duty not to use persons as mere means.
  SUPPORT: (1) the separateness-of-persons objection; (2) the epistemic objection
           (we cannot compute the aggregates reliably).
  STRONGEST OBJECTION: rule-utilitarianism captures the duty-like constraint
           while keeping consequences primary.
example.walkthrough: The prospectus is a cheap test of an expensive commitment: if the shape does not hold in 200 words, it will not hold in 1,500.

pitfalls: Choosing a thesis so broad it needs a book, not a paper.
Picking a thesis nobody could disagree with — no opposition means no argument.
Skipping the prospectus and 'discovering' the structure mid-draft.
lessons.try_it: Write your 200-word prospectus today; if the strongest objection is blank, the thesis is not ready.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 2 — Research, Steelman, and Anticipate Objections
concepts: Research primary moves, not summaries: read the actual argument (even a chapter or a classic paper's core section), not just what someone said about it. One primary source beats five encyclopedia glosses.
Steelman the opposition: write the best version of the other side's case — the version its smartest defender would endorse. Your replies are only as strong as the objection they defeat.
Anticipate at least two objections: one internal (a tension inside your own framework) and one external (a rival framework's attack). Papers die on the objection they never saw coming.
For each objection, draft the reply before writing the paper: concede what is true in it, then show why it does not defeat the thesis. Concession disarms; evasion invites.

example.code:
Objection-handling template:
  OBJECTION (external): A utilitarian replies that rule-utilitarianism...
  CONCEDE: It is true that...
  REPLY: ...but this still fails because...
  UPGRADE: Even granting the objection, the thesis survives in weakened form: ...
example.walkthrough: Conceding the true part of an objection is not weakness — it is how you show the examiner you understand the objection well enough to survive it.

pitfalls: Attacking strawmen: the weakest version of the opposition. Examiners spot this instantly.
Researching only sources that agree with you — confirmation is not research.
Listing objections without replies. An unanswered objection is a concession.
lessons.try_it: Write the steelman of your opposition's best argument in 150 words — then hand it to a friend and ask if the other side would accept it.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 3 — Draft, Defend, and Revise
concepts: Structure the paper: introduction with thesis stated plainly; exposition of your arguments (one per section); the strongest objection fairly stated; your replies; conclusion restating what was shown. Signpost constantly.
One idea per paragraph, one argument per section. If a paragraph contains two arguments, split it. Examiners reward clarity of structure as much as depth of content.
Defend it aloud: explain your thesis and survive questions for ten minutes. Every stumble marks a paragraph that needs rewriting — speech exposes hand-waving that prose hides.
Revise in passes: pass one for argument structure, pass two for objections and replies, pass three for prose. Never revise prose before the arguments are sound.

example.code:
Revision checklist:
  [ ] Thesis stated in the first paragraph, in one sentence
  [ ] Each section argues exactly one claim
  [ ] Strongest objection stated fairly (opponent would accept it)
  [ ] Every objection gets an explicit reply
  [ ] Conclusion claims only what the arguments established
example.walkthrough: The checklist is merciless on purpose: most lost marks come from structure (missing replies, blurred thesis), not from insufficient cleverness.

pitfalls: Burying the thesis on page three. State it first, defend it after.
Ending with 'more research is needed' instead of a conclusion that claims the result.
Polishing sentences before the argument structure is settled.
lessons.try_it: Do a ten-minute spoken defense of your thesis today; rewrite every paragraph where you stumbled.

lessons.title: The Presocratics: Nature Without Gods
concepts: The Presocratics asked what everything is made of and refused mythological answers: Thales proposed water, Anaximenes air, Heraclitus fire and flux — the first naturalistic explanations.
Parmenides argued change is impossible: being is one, unchanging, and indivisible; appearances of motion are illusion. His logic forced every later thinker to answer him.
Heraclitus answered with flux: you cannot step in the same river twice — reality is process, held together by the logos (rational order).
Democritus proposed atoms and the void: indivisible particles moving in empty space explain all change mechanically — a startling anticipation of physical explanation without purpose.

example.code:
Parmenides' core move:
  1. What is, is; what is not, cannot be thought or spoken.
  2. Change would require what-is to come from what-is-not.
  3. Therefore change is impossible; being is one and motionless.
  The power is in premise 1: try to deny it without referring to nothing.
example.walkthrough: Parmenides shows how a valid argument from plausible premises can reach an insane conclusion — which is why later philosophers attacked his premises (pluralists) or his logic rather than shrugging.

pitfalls: Treating the Presocratics as primitive. Their questions — what is fundamental, is change real — are still live.
Quoting Heraclitus' river without the logos: flux alone is chaos; his point was order within change.
Assuming Democritus' atoms are modern atoms. His are philosophical: indivisible by definition, not by experiment.
lessons.try_it: Reconstruct Parmenides' argument in your own words, then write the one premise you would attack.

lessons.title: Socrates and the Examined Life
concepts: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Plato's dialogues. His method, the elenchus, cross-examines someone's beliefs until contradiction surfaces — refutation as a path to truth.
Socratic ignorance: 'I know that I know nothing' is not modesty but method — recognizing ignorance is the precondition for inquiry, and most people fail at this first step.
'Virtue is knowledge': Socrates argued no one does wrong knowingly — wrongdoing comes from ignorance of the good. This intellectualism about ethics is bold, strange, and worth wrestling with.
The examined life: at his trial (Apology), Socrates chose death over silence, claiming 'the unexamined life is not worth living' — philosophy as a way of life, not a subject.

example.code:
The elenchus in three moves:
  1. Ask for a definition ('What is courage?').
  2. Draw out consequences the interlocutor accepts.
  3. Show the consequences contradict the definition.
  Result: refutation (elenchus), not a new definition — clearing ground.
example.walkthrough: The elenchus rarely produces a positive theory; its product is aporia (puzzlement). That is the point: false confidence destroyed is progress, because inquiry can finally begin.

pitfalls: Thinking Socratic ignorance means knowing literally nothing. It means knowing the limits of what you know.
Treating the elenchus as just 'asking questions.' It is adversarial testing of consistency, not curiosity.
Reading the Apology as martyrdom theater. It is a philosophical defense of a way of life.
lessons.try_it: Run a 5-minute elenchus on one of your own beliefs: define it, draw consequences, hunt for contradiction.

lessons.title: Plato: Forms and the Cave
concepts: The Theory of Forms: the physical world is a shadow of perfect, eternal, unchanging Forms (Justice itself, Beauty itself). Particulars participate in Forms imperfectly.

The Cave allegory (Republic VII): prisoners see shadows, mistake them for reality; the freed prisoner ascends to the sun (the Form of the Good) and returns to free the others — philosophy as painful enlightenment plus obligation.
The tripartite soul: reason, spirit, appetite. Justice in the soul — and in the city — is each part doing its proper work under reason's rule.
Philosopher-kings: only those who grasp the Forms should rule, because only they know the Good. Radically anti-democratic, and meant to provoke: is expertise in the good real?

example.code:
The divided line (Republic):
  IMAGINATION (shadows) < BELIEF (physical things) < THOUGHT (mathematics) < UNDERSTANDING (Forms)
  Ascending = moving from images to the realities they image. The cave is this line dramatized.
example.walkthrough: Plato's move is to explain stability of knowledge: mathematics and morals seem objective, but physical things change — so their objects must be non-physical. Attack that inference and you attack Platonism.

pitfalls: Reading the cave as 'ignorant people vs smart people.' It is about the structure of reality and the duty to return, not IQ.
Treating Forms as 'concepts in the mind.' They are mind-independent realities for Plato — the mind discovers, not invents.
Missing that the philosopher must go back down. Enlightenment without obligation is not Plato's vision.
lessons.try_it: Map one modern case (e.g., social media) onto the cave: what are the shadows, the fire, the ascent?

lessons.title: Aristotle: Logic, Causes, and Virtue
concepts: Aristotle invented formal logic: the syllogism ('All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal') systematized valid inference for two millennia.

The four causes: material (what it is made of), formal (its structure), efficient (what made it), final (its purpose/end). Full explanation requires all four — modern science kept three and dropped the final cause.
Virtue ethics: eudaimonia (flourishing) is the goal; virtues are habits of choosing the mean between excess and deficiency (courage between cowardice and recklessness).
The function argument: a thing's good is performing its function well; the human function is rational activity — so the good life is rational activity done excellently (with virtue).

example.code:
The golden mean is not mediocrity:
  DEFICIENCY ---- MEAN ---- EXCESS
  cowardice --- COURAGE --- recklessness
  stinginess -- GENEROSITY -- wastefulness
  The mean is 'relative to us' — context-sensitive, found by practical wisdom (phronesis), not arithmetic.
example.walkthrough: Aristotle's ethics is anti-formula: the mean shifts with circumstances, which is why virtue needs phronesis (practical wisdom) rather than a rulebook. That flexibility is the theory's strength and its vulnerability.

pitfalls: Treating the mean as 'always pick the middle.' It is the right amount for the situation, which is sometimes extreme.
Reading the four causes as four competing theories. They are four complementary answers to 'why?'
Assuming Aristotle's logic is obsolete. Syllogistic is limited, but validity-as-form starts here.
lessons.try_it: Take one virtue (e.g., honesty) and specify its excess, deficiency, and mean in a concrete situation.

lessons.title: Hellenistic Schools: How to Live
concepts: After Aristotle, philosophy turned practical: Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Skepticism all promise tranquility (ataraxia) amid a chaotic world — philosophy as therapy.
Stoicism (Zeno, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius): distinguish what is up to us (judgments, intentions) from what is not (everything else); assent only to true impressions; live according to nature/reason.

Epicureanism: pleasure is the good, but understood as absence of pain and disturbance — simple pleasures, friendship, and the famous arguments that death is nothing to us ('when we exist, death is not; when death exists, we are not').
Skepticism (Pyrrho, Sextus Empiricus): suspend judgment on undecidable questions; equipollence — for every argument there is an equal counter-argument — leads to tranquility.

example.code:
The Stoic dichotomy of control (Epictetus, Enchiridion):
  UP TO US: opinion, intention, desire, aversion — our own actions
  NOT UP TO US: body, property, reputation, office — everything else
  Rule: invest your effort in the first list; accept the second.
example.walkthrough: The schools disagree about the good (virtue vs pleasure vs suspension) but agree on the method: philosophy must change how you live, or it is empty. That practical test still judges philosophical theories today.

pitfalls: Reading Stoicism as emotion suppression. It is judgment correction: emotions follow assents, so examine the assent.
Reading Epicureanism as indulgence. It is the most disciplined hedonism ever devised — simple pleasures only.
Treating Skeptic suspension as apathy. It is a technique for tranquility, not indifference to truth.
lessons.try_it: Apply the dichotomy of control to one current anxiety: sort its elements into the two lists.

lessons.title: Ontology: What Exists?
concepts: Ontology asks what there is and what it means to exist. Realists say abstract things (numbers, properties) exist mind-independently; nominalists say only particulars exist and 'redness' is just a word for resembling particulars.

Quine's criterion: 'to be is to be the value of a bound variable' — your ontology is what your best theories quantify over. Ontological commitment is read off from what you say exists, not from vibes.

Meinongianism takes the radical route: there are things that do not exist (the golden mountain, the round square) — we can talk about them, so in some sense they have being. Most philosophers find this too costly.
The debate matters practically: are corporations, nations, and software 'real'? Your answer shapes law, economics, and how you count things in models.

example.code:
The nominalist's challenge:
  'Show me redness.' You point to a red apple.
  'That's an apple, not redness. Point to redness itself.'
  Realist reply: resemblance itself needs explaining — what makes
  two red things similar? The shared universal: redness.
example.walkthrough: Quine's criterion is the great clarifier: stop asking 'is X real?' in the abstract and ask 'does our best theory need to quantify over X?' If yes, you are committed to X whether you like it or not.

pitfalls: Treating 'exists' as one flat notion. Meinong shows it might split (being vs existence).
Thinking nominalism denies patterns. It denies universals, not similarities — it just explains them differently (tropes, resemblance classes).
Assuming the debate has no stakes. It decides what your theories are committed to.
lessons.try_it: List five things your worldview quantifies over (numbers? minds? corporations?) — that list is your ontology.

lessons.title: Causation and Laws of Nature
concepts: Hume's challenge: we never observe causation itself, only constant conjunction — A followed by B, repeatedly. 'Necessary connection' is a habit of the mind projected onto the world, not something seen.
Humeanism about laws: laws are just regularities — summaries of the mosaic of events. Necessitarianism: laws govern, constraining what can happen; causation is real production, not mere correlation.
Counterfactual theories (Lewis): C causes E if, had C not occurred, E would not have occurred. This handles many cases elegantly but struggles with overdetermination (two fires, either sufficient).
Why it matters: every regression, every A/B test, every 'X causes Y' claim in science and policy assumes an account of causation. Hume's ghost haunts all of them.

example.code:
Overdetermination vs preemption:
  OVERDETERMINATION: two assassins shoot simultaneously; either bullet
    alone would kill. Counterfactual 'if A hadn't shot, victim lives' fails.
  PREEMPTION: A shoots; B would have shot if A missed. A's shot caused
    the death, though the counterfactual fails (victim dies anyway).
example.walkthrough: Causation looks simple until you formalize it — then every theory meets a counterexample. The exam skill is not picking the winner but diagnosing exactly which cases break which theory.

pitfalls: Confusing correlation with causation — Hume's whole point is that observation gives you the first, and the second needs an argument.
Thinking counterfactuals solve everything. Overdetermination and preemption are the standard killers.
Assuming 'law of nature' means 'legislated.' The metaphor misleads: Humeans deny any lawgiver-like necessity.
lessons.try_it: Take one causal claim from the news and state which theory of causation it presupposes.

lessons.title: Free Will: Compatibilism and Its Rivals
concepts: The problem: if every event has a sufficient cause (determinism), how can choices be 'up to us'? Incompatibilists say they cannot — hence libertarianism (we have undetermined free choice) or hard determinism (we do not).
Compatibilism: freedom is acting from your own desires and character without external compulsion — determinism is compatible with this. Hobbes, Hume, and Frankfurt defend versions.

Frankfurt's intervener: Black will force Jones to act if Jones wavers, but Jones acts on his own — Black never intervenes. Jones is responsible though he 'could not have done otherwise.' So responsibility does not need alternative possibilities.

The consequence argument (van Inwagen) pushes back: if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the distant past plus laws — things we cannot change — so we are not responsible. This is incompatibilism's strongest weapon.

example.code:
Frankfurt cases, schematized:
  Jones decides to do A on his own.
  Black monitors: if Jones wavers, Black forces A.
  Jones never wavers; Black does nothing.
  Intuition: Jones is responsible for A.
  Upshot: moral responsibility does not require could-have-done-otherwise.
example.walkthrough: Frankfurt reframes the debate: stop asking 'was the act undetermined?' and ask 'did it flow from the agent's own will?' That shift — from metaphysics of alternatives to the structure of agency — is why the paper is endlessly cited.

pitfalls: Thinking compatibilism denies determinism. It accepts it and redefines freedom.
Confusing Frankfurt's point: it targets the principle of alternative possibilities, not determinism directly.
Assuming 'could have done otherwise' is obviously required for responsibility. That is the thesis under dispute.
lessons.try_it: Construct your own Frankfurt case with a contemporary setting (an algorithm, not a neuroscientist).

lessons.title: Identity Through Time
concepts: The Ship of Theseus: every plank replaced over years — same ship? Then the discarded planks are reassembled elsewhere — which is the ship? Identity through change resists simple answers.
Endurantism: objects are wholly present at each time (a 3D object moving through time). Perdurantism: objects are 4D worms with temporal parts — the ship is the sum of its ship-stages.
Personal identity theories: bodily continuity (same body), psychological continuity (memory chains — Locke, Parfit), soul theory. Each handles some puzzle cases and breaks on others.

Parfit's fission: your brain hemispheres go into two bodies, both psychologically continuous with you. Identity cannot split (one person cannot be two), so what matters is continuity, not identity — a revisionary, influential result.

example.code:
Locke's prince and the cobbler:
  A prince's memories enter a cobbler's body (and vice versa).
  Intuition: the prince goes with the memories.
  Lesson: personhood tracks psychology, not the body —
  until fission cases show even psychology breaks down.
example.walkthrough: Puzzle cases are diagnostic tools: they do not refute theories so much as reveal their commitments. The exam skill is saying 'this case forces theory T to accept consequence C' — mapping costs, not picking winners.

pitfalls: Demanding one theory handle all cases. The field's lesson is that identity might be the wrong question (Parfit).
Treating the ship puzzle as a trick. It exposes that 'same' is ambiguous: same planks vs same continuity.
Forgetting the practical stakes: identity grounds responsibility, ownership, and survival.
lessons.try_it: Design a puzzle case that breaks YOUR preferred theory of personal identity, then state the cost.

lessons.title: Time and Modality
concepts: A-theory (tensed): past, present, future are real metaphysical divisions; time flows. B-theory (tenseless): only earlier/later relations are real; 'now' is perspectival, like 'here.' Physics leans B-theory; experience screams A-theory.
Presentism: only the present exists. Eternalism: past, present, and future all exist (the block universe). Growing block: past and present exist; the future does not — yet.

Possible worlds (Lewis): modality is quantification over concrete worlds — 'possibly P' means P holds in some world. Genuine modal realism: those worlds are as real as ours. Most find this extravagant; all use the semantics.

Time travel paradoxes test the views: the grandfather paradox threatens consistency; Lewis's reply — time travelers can act but cannot change the past (compossibility) — shows how modal metaphysics disciplines science fiction.

example.code:
McTaggart's argument against time:
  A-series (past/present/future) is essential to time.
  Every event has all three A-properties (future, then present, then past).
  Having incompatible properties is contradictory — unless relativized to times.
  But relativizing ('was future') just reintroduces the A-series. Contradiction stands.
  Conclusion: time is unreal. (Most reject a premise; which one?)
example.walkthrough: McTaggart is the perfect exam specimen: a short, valid-looking argument to an insane conclusion. Your job is never to accept it but to locate the premise to deny — and every live theory of time is, in effect, an answer to McTaggart.

pitfalls: Treating 'the present' as scientifically settled. Relativity of simultaneity is the B-theorist's best friend.
Dismissing Lewis's worlds as fantasy while using possible-worlds talk. The semantics needs the ontology question answered, not dodged.
Thinking time travel is just physics. The paradoxes are metaphysical: consistency constraints on any coherent story.
lessons.try_it: State whether you are an A-theorist or B-theorist and name the hardest datum for your side.

lessons.title: Propositional Logic: The Machinery
concepts: Propositions are truth-bearers (statements that are true or false). Connectives — not, and, or, if-then, iff — build complex propositions from simple ones, with meaning fixed by truth tables.

Validity is formal: an argument is valid iff no assignment makes the premises true and the conclusion false. The truth table is a decision procedure — mechanical, complete, and boring in the best way.

Key valid forms: modus ponens (if P then Q; P; so Q), modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; so not P), disjunctive syllogism. Key invalid form: affirming the consequent (if P then Q; Q; so P) — the most seductive fallacy in the wild.

Material conditional quirk: 'if P then Q' is false only when P is true and Q false — so 'if the moon is cheese then I am king' is true (vacuously). Weird but precise; do not import everyday 'if' intuitions.

example.code:
Modus tollens in the wild:
  P1: If the server is down, the dashboard is red.
  P2: The dashboard is not red.
  C: The server is not down. (valid)
  Contrast — affirming the consequent:
  P2': The dashboard IS red. C': The server is down. (INVALID —
  red dashboards have many causes)
example.walkthrough: Modus tollens is the scientist's workhorse: theories imply predictions; failed prediction kills the theory. Affirming the consequent is the corresponding vice: successful prediction merely fails to kill it.

pitfalls: Reading 'if P then Q' as 'P causes Q.' The material conditional is truth-functional, not causal.
Thinking validity is about true premises. The truth table checks form across ALL assignments.
Confusing 'invalid' with 'false conclusion.' Invalid arguments can have true conclusions — by luck.
lessons.try_it: Write three modus tollens arguments about systems you manage; then write the affirming-the-consequent version of each and feel the difference.

lessons.title: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
concepts: Predicate logic adds quantifiers: ∀x (for all x) and ∃x (there exists an x), plus predicates and relations. 'All servers are monitored' becomes ∀x(Server(x) → Monitored(x)).
Scope matters enormously: ∀x∃y Loves(x,y) (everyone loves someone) vs ∃y∀x Loves(x,y) (someone is loved by everyone) — different claims, different truth conditions.
Quantifier negation: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) ('not all are monitored' = 'some server is unmonitored'). This equivalence is the engine of precise denial.
Syllogisms are predicate logic fragments: 'All M are P; all S are M; so all S are P' is ∀x(M(x)→P(x)), ∀x(S(x)→M(x)) ⊢ ∀x(S(x)→P(x)) — Aristotle's logic as a special case.

example.code:
Scope ambiguity in policy:
  'Every engineer has access to a production database.'
  Reading 1: ∀e∃d (each engineer has some prod DB — maybe different ones)
  Reading 2: ∃d∀e (there is ONE prod DB every engineer can access)
  Reading 2 is a security incident; Reading 1 might be fine. Disambiguate!
example.walkthrough: Scope ambiguity is where security policies and contracts silently break: the English hides two logical forms with different consequences. Formalizing forces the choice.

pitfalls: Assuming quantifier order does not matter. It almost always does.
Translating 'some' as 'at least one' correctly but then treating it as 'most.' ∃ means one or more — nothing more.
Negating ∀x P(x) as ∀x ¬P(x). The negation flips the quantifier: ∃x ¬P(x).
lessons.try_it: Formalize two sentences from your team's runbooks and check for scope ambiguity.

lessons.title: Induction, Abduction, Analogy
concepts: Deduction preserves truth (valid = conclusion must follow); induction amplifies (premises make conclusion probable — enumerative: all observed swans are white, so all swans are white). Strength, not validity, is the standard.

Abduction is inference to the best explanation: the dashboard is red, the deploy just landed, deploys often break things — the best explanation is the deploy. Diagnosis, debugging, and science run on abduction.
Abductive virtues: explanatory power, simplicity, coherence with background knowledge, predictive novelty. 'Best' is comparative — always ask 'best among which rivals?'

Analogy: A and B share features; A has feature F; so B probably has F. Strength depends on relevant similarity and absence of relevant difference — analogies persuade by mapping structure, and die on disanalogy.

example.code:
Abduction in incident response:
  OBSERVED: latency spikes every hour at :00.
  CANDIDATE 1: cron job (simple, fits the periodicity).
  CANDIDATE 2: cosmic rays (explains nothing about :00).
  INFERENCE: investigate the cron jobs first — best explanation wins
  the first hour of debugging.
example.walkthrough: Abduction is defeasible: new evidence can overturn it. That is not a flaw — it is the logic of working under uncertainty, which is where all real reasoning happens.

pitfalls: Demanding deductive certainty from inductive arguments. The standard is strength, and strength comes in degrees.
Treating the best explanation as the true one. It is the best-supported bet — keep the rivals alive.
Judging analogies by surface similarity. What matters is structural/causal similarity.
lessons.try_it: Take your last production incident and reconstruct it as an abductive argument: observations, rival explanations, winning virtues.

lessons.title: Fallacies: The Rogues' Gallery
concepts: Ad hominem: attacking the arguer instead of the argument ('you would say that, you're an engineer'). The argument's validity never depends on who states it.
Strawman: refuting a weakened version of the opponent's position. The tell: the opponent would not recognize their view in your description (see the steelman lesson).
Begging the question: smuggling the conclusion into the premises ('this policy is fair because it treats everyone fairly' — but is it fair? That was the question).
