Equivocation: shifting a word's meaning mid-argument ('banks hold money; river banks hold water; so rivers hold money'). Also: slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to authority/nature/popularity — learn the tells, not just the names.

example.code:
Spot the fallacy:
  'We must not allow encrypted messaging, because criminals use
  encryption, and we must stop criminals.'
  Analysis: the premise (criminals use X) does not support banning X
  for everyone — non sequitur via suppressed premise ('anything criminals
  use should be banned'), which is absurd (criminals use roads).
example.walkthrough: Fallacy-spotting is diagnostic, not a refutation machine: naming the fallacy tells you where the argument breaks, but the charitable move is to ask whether a repaired version survives.

pitfalls: Using fallacy labels as insults ('that's ad hominem!') instead of diagnoses. Name the break, then check for a repair.
Memorizing names without the underlying pattern. The pattern is what recurs; names are just handles.
Thinking fallacious arguments always have false conclusions. They can be right for bad reasons.
lessons.try_it: Find three fallacies in today's online discourse; for each, write the repaired (strongest) version of the argument.

lessons.title: Argument Mapping in Practice
concepts: An argument map lays out premises, hidden premises, objections, and replies as a tree: conclusion at top, supporting premises below, objections attached to the exact claim they target.
Step one is always: find the conclusion. Indicator words help ('therefore,' 'so,' 'hence') but authors hide conclusions; ask 'what is this person trying to get me to believe?'

Expose hidden premises: most real arguments are enthymemes (incomplete). 'We should ban X because criminals use X' hides 'whatever criminals use should be banned' — surfacing it is often the whole critique.
Apply charity last: once mapped, strengthen the argument before attacking (steelman). A map of a strawman is wasted work.

example.code:
Mini-map:
  [C] Deploy should be rolled back.
    +-- [P1] Error rate spiked 10x after deploy. (evidence: dashboard)
    +-- [P2, hidden] A 10x error spike outweighs any benefit of the deploy.
    +-- [OBJ] The spike is from a botnet, not the deploy. (targets P1's link)
         +-- [REPLY] Botnet traffic predates the deploy by 6h. (evidence: logs)
example.walkthrough: The map's discipline is targeting: objections attach to specific premises, so you see exactly which claim is under attack and what would save it. Verbal debates blur this; maps do not.

pitfalls: Mapping the conclusion as just another premise. The conclusion is the root; everything else serves it.
Attaching objections to the whole argument instead of the premise they hit. Precision is the point.
Skipping hidden premises. The hidden premise is where real arguments live and die.
lessons.try_it: Map one argument from a design doc or postmortem this week, exposing at least one hidden premise.

lessons.title: Dualism: Descartes and After
concepts: Substance dualism (Descartes): mind and body are distinct substances — thinking, unextended mind vs extended, unthinking matter. The pineal gland was his (bad) guess at their interface.

The interaction problem: if mind is non-physical, how does it move the body? Princess Elisabeth pressed Descartes on this: contact requires extension, which mind lacks. Every dualism since is an answer to Elisabeth.

Property dualism retreats: one substance (the brain) with two kinds of properties — physical and irreducibly mental (qualia). Saves interaction at the cost of explaining how one substance hosts two property kinds.

Why dualism persists: consciousness feels non-physical from the inside. Any theory must either explain that feeling away or take it seriously — dualism takes it seriously at maximum metaphysical cost.

example.code:
Elisabeth's challenge (1643):
  'How can the soul move the body, given that motion requires
  contact, and contact requires extension — which the soul,
  being unextended, lacks?'
  Descartes never gave a satisfactory answer. The problem named
  here still structures the entire field.
example.walkthrough: Elisabeth's question is the perfect philosophical objection: short, principled, and fatal to the letter of the theory. Every later position — from property dualism to physicalism — can be read as an attempt to answer her.

pitfalls: Treating dualism as refuted by neuroscience. Correlation (brain damage affects mind) does not refute distinctness — it is compatible with interaction.
Confusing substance and property dualism. They face different problems and pay different costs.
Thinking the interaction problem is just 'we haven't found the mechanism.' It is principled: the categories seem to forbid interaction.
lessons.try_it: State Elisabeth's objection in your own words, then give dualism's best one-line reply.

lessons.title: Physicalism: Identity Theory and Eliminativism
concepts: Identity theory (Smart, Place): mental states ARE brain states — pain = C-fiber firing. Not correlation, identity: like lightning = electrical discharge.

The multiple-realizability objection (Putnam): pain in octopuses, humans, and (hypothetically) Martians shares the mental kind but not the brain state — so mental kinds cannot be identical to specific neural kinds.

Eliminativism (Churchlands): 'belief,' 'desire,' 'pain' are folk-psychological posits that a mature neuroscience will eliminate, like 'phlogiston' was eliminated. Radical, bracing, and rarely believed — but hard to refute cheaply.

The dialectic: identity theory is too chauvinistic (only our neurons can think), eliminativism too revisionary (your headache is a theoretical posit?). Functionalism was built to split the difference.

example.code:
Multiple realizability, schematized:
  Pain in humans: C-fibers firing.
  Pain in octopuses: totally different neurology.
  Same mental kind (pain), different physical kinds.
  Therefore: pain != C-fiber firing. (Identity theory fails.)
  Upshot: mental kinds are functional kinds, not neural kinds.
example.walkthrough: Multiple realizability is the most influential objection in philosophy of mind: it moves the field from 'which neurons?' to 'which functional role?' in one step. Learn to wield it — and to spot its limits (maybe Martian pain is not pain).

pitfalls: Reading identity theory as 'mind correlates with brain.' It claims identity — stronger, and stronger claims break easier.
Dismissing eliminativism as silly. Its argument (folk theory has a bad track record) deserves an answer, not a laugh.
Thinking multiple realizability refutes physicalism. It refutes type-identity; token-identity and functionalism survive.
lessons.try_it: Give the best reply open to the identity theorist against multiple realizability (hint: species-specific identities).

lessons.title: Functionalism: The Mind as Software
concepts: Functionalism (Putnam, Lewis): mental states are functional states — defined by their causal role (inputs, outputs, relations to other states), not their physical substrate. Mind is to brain as software is to hardware.

Multiple realizability becomes a feature: silicon, neurons, or Martian goo can all realize pain if they play the pain-role. This is why functionalism dominates cognitive science and AI-adjacent philosophy.

Machine functionalism vs causal-role functionalism: the first models mind as a Turing machine's states; the second defines each mental state by its typical causes and effects (pain = caused by damage, causes avoidance).

The absent-qualia objection: a functional duplicate of you (same inputs/outputs) might lack inner experience — a zombie. If conceivable, function does not suffice for feeling. The hard problem knocks.

example.code:
The Turing-machine model of mind:
  STATE S1 + INPUT 'damage' -> OUTPUT 'wince', move to S2
  Pain = being in the state that plays this causal role.
  Substrate irrelevant: neurons, chips, or (Putnam's image)
  a Swiss-cheese brain — if it computes the transitions, it minds.
example.walkthrough: Functionalism's genius is making substrate independence principled: what matters is the pattern of causal relations, which is why the same psychology can run on different hardware — and why AI systems are the live test case.

pitfalls: Treating functionalism as 'the brain is literally a computer.' It is the weaker, precise claim: mental states are individuated by causal role.
Assuming functionalism explains qualia. Its critics say it explains everything except what it is like — the hard problem.
Confusing the software/hardware analogy with an identity claim. It is an analogy for role-vs-substrate, not a metaphysics.
lessons.try_it: Describe a functional duplicate of yourself that you suspect would lack consciousness — then state what your suspicion commits you to.

lessons.title: Consciousness: The Hard Problem
concepts: Chalmers' distinction: the easy problems (report, attention, control — mechanisms) vs the hard problem: why is any of it accompanied by subjective experience — what it is like to see red?
Qualia: the qualitative character of experience. Inverted spectrum: your red might be my green, with all behavior identical — if conceivable, qualia outrun function.

Mary the color scientist (Jackson): knows all physical facts about color vision while confined to black-and-white; on release, seeing red, she learns something new — what red looks like. So not all facts are physical facts.

Zombies (Chalmers): a physical duplicate of you with no inner life is conceivable; if conceivable, consciousness does not supervene on the physical with metaphysical necessity — physicalism is incomplete.

example.code:
Mary's room, compressed:
  P1: Mary knows every physical fact about color vision.
  P2: On seeing red, she learns a new fact (what red looks like).
  C: Some facts are not physical facts.
  Physicalist replies: deny P2 ('ability,' not fact — Lewis/Nemirow),
  or deny P1 (she didn't know ALL the physical facts).
example.walkthrough: Mary is the cleanest argument in the field: two premises, massive conclusion. Every physicalist must deny a premise — and each denial has a cost. Learn the reply menu; it recurs for zombies and inverted spectra too.

pitfalls: Treating the hard problem as 'consciousness is mysterious.' It is precise: why does function come with feeling?
Thinking zombies are claimed to exist. The claim is conceivability → metaphysical possibility → physicalism incomplete.
Assuming Mary refutes science. It targets reductive physicalism's completeness claim, not neuroscience.
lessons.try_it: Pick one physicalist reply to Mary and state its cost in one sentence.

lessons.title: Intentionality and Content
concepts: Intentionality (Brentano): mental states are about things — beliefs point beyond themselves. Brentano called this the mark of the mental; physical things are not 'about' anything.

The Chinese room (Searle): a person manipulating Chinese symbols by rulebook produces perfect replies with zero understanding — syntax is not semantics. Running the right program does not suffice for understanding.

Responses: the systems reply (the whole room understands), the robot reply (ground symbols in sensorimotor interaction), the brain-simulator reply. Searle's counter: the man internalizes the rulebook — still no understanding.
Why it matters for AI: every claim that a chatbot 'understands' inherits this debate. The room isolates the variable — hold behavior fixed, remove comprehension — and asks what is left.

example.code:
Searle's internalization move:
  'Suppose I memorize the rulebook and do the manipulations
  in my head. I still don't understand Chinese.'
  Target: the systems reply ('the system understands').
  If the man IS the system and understands nothing,
  the system understands nothing.
example.walkthrough: The dialectic here is a masterclass in objection-and-reply: each response to Searle gets a Searlean counter, and the field's positions are defined by where they exit the loop. Track the loop, not just the opening move.

pitfalls: Reading the room as 'AI can never work.' It targets a specific claim: computation suffices for understanding.
Treating behavioral success as settling the question. The room's point is that behavior underdetermines understanding.
Missing that Searle grants the program works. His claim is about what running it amounts to.
lessons.try_it: Grant Searle the room; now state the strongest reply and Searle's counter to it.

lessons.title: The Social Contract: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau
concepts: Hobbes (Leviathan): the state of nature is war of all against all — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' We authorize an absolute sovereign to escape it; justice is keeping the contract that peace requires.

Locke: the state of nature is inconvenient, not war — we have natural rights (life, liberty, property). Government by consent protects them; when it violates them systematically, revolution is justified.
Rousseau: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' The social contract must express the general will — each obeys only the law they prescribe to themselves; that is freedom under law.
The contract is hypothetical, not historical: the question is what free, rational people WOULD agree to — a justificatory device, not an anthropology claim. Attack the justification, not the history.

example.code:
Three states of nature, one question:
  HOBBES: war -> need: any sovereign strong enough for peace.
  LOCKE: inconvenience -> need: limited government guarding rights.
  ROUSSEAU: corruption by society -> need: contract expressing general will.
  Same device, different anthropology, different politics.
example.walkthrough: The state of nature is a thought experiment about justification: describe humans without government, derive what government they would rationally accept. The politics follows from the anthropology — which is why the descriptions differ so sharply.

pitfalls: Treating the contract as a historical event. No signer, no parchment — it is a justificatory thought experiment.
Reading Hobbes as pro-tyranny. He is pro-whatever-ends-civil-war; the sovereign's absoluteness is instrumental to peace.
Missing Rousseau's freedom paradox: obeying the general will (including when outvoted) counts as obeying yourself. Wrestle with it.
lessons.try_it: Write the state-of-nature description that YOUR politics presupposes, then derive your ideal government from it.

lessons.title: Justice as Fairness: Rawls
concepts: The veil of ignorance: design society's basic structure without knowing your place in it — class, talent, gender, generation. Fair principles are the ones rational agents would choose blind.

The two principles: (1) equal basic liberties for all, with priority over other goods; (2) social and economic inequalities allowed only if (a) attached to fair equality of opportunity and (b) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle).

The difference principle is the radical edge: inequality is justified only by improving the worst-off position — not by total growth, not by desert. Talent is morally arbitrary; its rewards must serve everyone.

Reflective equilibrium: we test principles against considered judgments (e.g., 'slavery is unjust') and revise both ways until they cohere. Justification is mutual adjustment, not derivation from axioms.

example.code:
Applying the veil:
  You don't know if you'll be born talented or disabled, rich or poor.
  Would you gamble on winner-take-all? Or insure yourself with the
  difference principle — inequalities only if they lift the bottom?
  Rawls bets rational agents are risk-averse about their whole life.
example.walkthrough: The veil operationalizes impartiality: it turns 'be fair' into a decision procedure. Every policy proposal can be run through it — which is why the device outlives Rawls's specific principles.

pitfalls: Treating the veil as 'pretend you are poor.' It is stronger: you might be anyone, including the least advantaged — design accordingly.
Reading the difference principle as equality of outcome. It permits inequality — conditionally, and the condition bites.
Missing the priority of liberty: no trading basic freedoms for economic gains, however large.
lessons.try_it: Run one real policy (e.g., school funding by property tax) through the veil; state the verdict.

lessons.title: Libertarianism: Nozick's Reply
concepts: Nozick's entitlement theory: a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to their holdings — justice in acquisition, justice in transfer, rectification of past injustice. No patterned end-state required.

The Wilt Chamberlain argument: start from any 'just' patterned distribution; Wilt signs a contract giving him 25 cents per ticket; fans pay voluntarily; the pattern is destroyed by liberty. 'Liberty upsets patterns' — patterned justice requires continuous interference.

Taxation as forced labor (the provocative version): taxing earnings from voluntary exchange is morally akin to forcing extra labor for others' benefit. Meant to shift the burden: why is partial slavery okay?

The best Rawlsian reply: the parties behind the veil would not choose Nozick's minimal state — they would insure against being the worst-off. The debate is ultimately about risk attitudes under the veil.

example.code:
Wilt Chamberlain, step by step:
  D1: some distribution Rawls calls just.
  + voluntary transfers: 1M fans pay Wilt $0.25 each.
  D2: Wilt has $250,000 more; the pattern is broken.
  Each transfer was just (consenting adults).
  So: no patterned principle can survive liberty — justice must be
  historical (how holdings came about), not end-state.
example.walkthrough: Wilt is the cleanest objection in political philosophy: three steps from a granted premise to the denial of patterned justice. Rawlsians must either bite a bullet (forbid the transfers — illiberal) or show the pattern can be maintained without illiberal means.

pitfalls: Reading Nozick as defending current distributions. Entitlement theory condemns holdings from unjust acquisition — rectification is the radical, unfinished part.
Thinking Wilt refutes all redistribution. It targets patterned end-state theories specifically.
Missing that Nozick grants a minimal state (protection, enforcement). He is not an anarchist.
lessons.try_it: State the strongest Rawlsian reply to Wilt in two sentences, then Nozick's counter.

lessons.title: Democracy and Liberty
concepts: Mill's harm principle (On Liberty): power may be exercised over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others. Self-regarding conduct — however foolish — is sovereign territory.

The epistemic defense of free speech: silencing an opinion robs humanity — if right, we lose truth; if wrong, we lose the clearer understanding truth gains by collision with error. Even true beliefs held unexamined are 'dead dogma.'

Democratic legitimacy puzzles: why should 51% rule 49%? Answers: consent, participation, epistemic (democracy tracks truth — Condorcet), or procedural fairness. Each faces the tyranny-of-the-majority worry.
Mill's own elitism: plural voting for the educated — democracy needs competent citizens, and competence is unequal. Democrats ever since have wrestled with this tension between equality and wisdom.

example.code:
The harm principle's hard cases:
  CLEAR: physical assault -> preventable.
  UNCLEAR: offense? economic competition? self-harm that grieves others?
  Mill's line: only conduct that harms (not merely offends) others
  licenses coercion. Every hard case is a fight over 'harm.'
example.walkthrough: The harm principle looks simple and dissolves on contact with hard cases — which is its philosophical interest. 'Harm' does all the work, so the real debate is the theory of harm hiding inside the slogan.

pitfalls: Treating the harm principle as libertarianism. Mill permits interference for harm prevention — a narrower but real license.
Reading Mill's free-speech defense as 'all opinions are equal.' It is epistemic: speech serves truth, and truth needs friction.
Ignoring the competence tension. Mill's plural voting shows even democrats fear ignorant majorities.
lessons.try_it: Take one speech controversy and decide it twice: once by the harm principle, once by the epistemic defense. Compare verdicts.

lessons.title: Power, Ideology, and Critique
concepts: Marx: alienation under capitalism — workers are estranged from the product, the process, their species-being, and each other. Ideology (including much philosophy) rationalizes the ruling class's interests as universal.

The base-superstructure model: economic relations shape law, politics, and ideas — not mechanically (vulgar Marxism), but as constraining and selecting. Ideas have relative autonomy; they are not mere reflections.

Foucault: power is not just top-down repression but productive — it shapes subjects through disciplines, norms, and knowledge ('power/knowledge'). The prison, the clinic, the school produce the modern individual.

Critique's method: unmask the contingent as necessary — show that what presents itself as natural (markets, gender roles, punishment) is historical and changeable. Genealogy traces how we became what we are.

example.code:
Alienation in four estrangements (Marx, 1844 Manuscripts):
  1. From the PRODUCT: it belongs to another, confronts you as alien.
  2. From the PROCESS: work is forced, not self-directed.
  3. From SPECIES-BEING: creative labor is human essence; denied it.
  4. From OTHERS: relations become competitive, instrumental.
  Test: does your work feel like self-expression or self-loss?
example.walkthrough: Critique differs from liberal reform: it does not ask how to distribute goods more fairly within the system but whether the system's categories (worker, owner, market) are themselves the problem. That is why it unsettles — and why it must answer the 'what then?' question.

pitfalls: Reducing Marx to 'communism good.' The analytical core is the critique of political economy — alienation, exploitation as defined, ideology.
Reading Foucault as 'everything is power, so nothing matters.' His point is that power is productive and local — hence resistible locally.
Treating genealogy as debunking by origin ('it came from power, so it's false'). Genesis does not settle validity — that would be the genetic fallacy.
lessons.try_it: Apply the four estrangements to one modern job (gig work, content moderation); note where the model fits and where it strains.

lessons.title: Exam Strategy: Reading the Question
concepts: Command words are instructions: 'explain' wants exposition of the argument; 'evaluate' wants exposition PLUS objections and replies; 'compare' wants mapped similarities and differences with a verdict.
'Evaluate' without objections is half an answer; 'explain' with objections wastes time. Match the structure to the verb — examiners check this first.
Scope words bound your answer: 'to what extent,' 'is X compatible with Y,' 'does P entail Q' — answer the exact relation asked, not the topic generally.
Plan before writing: 5 minutes mapping thesis → arguments → strongest objection → reply. Unplanned essays drift; planned essays argue.

example.code:
Question triage:
  'Explain Gettier's challenge to JTB.' -> exposition only. Structure:
    JTB -> two Gettier cases -> why luck breaks justification.
  'Evaluate Gettier's challenge.' -> exposition + objections
    (e.g., 'no-false-lemma' replies) + your verdict.
  Same topic, different verbs, different essays.
example.walkthrough: The verb is the rubric in miniature: it tells you which moves earn marks. Students lose the most marks not on content but on verb-mismatch — evaluating when asked to explain, or merely explaining when asked to evaluate.

pitfalls: Answering the topic instead of the question. The question's relation-words are the target.
Treating all questions as 'write everything you know about X.' Knowledge dumps score poorly.
Skipping the plan to 'save time.' The plan IS the time-saver.
lessons.try_it: Take three past questions and label each: verb, scope, and the essay structure it demands.

lessons.title: The Essay Skeleton
concepts: Introduction: state your thesis in one sentence, map the essay ('I will argue X by showing A and B, then answer the strongest objection'). No throat-clearing.
Exposition: reconstruct the target argument charitably — premises numbered, inference named. The examiner must see you understand before you criticize.
Objection and reply: state the STRONGEST objection fairly (opponent would accept it), then reply — concede what is true, defeat what is fatal. This section earns the top band.
Conclusion: restate what was shown — no new arguments, no 'more research is needed.' Claim exactly what the arguments established.

example.code:
Skeleton with word budget (1,500 words):
  Intro + thesis + map: 150
  Exposition of target argument: 400
  Your positive case: 400
  Strongest objection, fairly stated: 250
  Reply: 200
  Conclusion: 100
  The objection+reply block is 30% — budget accordingly.
example.walkthrough: The skeleton's discipline is proportion: students underweight objection-and-reply because it feels like helping the enemy. It is the opposite — surviving the strongest objection is what proves the thesis.

pitfalls: Hiding the thesis until the conclusion. State it first; defend it after.
New arguments in the conclusion. The conclusion summarizes; it does not argue.
Weak objections ('some might say...'). Name the strongest, or the section is theater.
lessons.try_it: Outline your next essay on this skeleton before writing a word; check the word budget per section.

lessons.title: Highest-Yield Distinctions
concepts: Validity vs soundness (form vs form+true premises); analytic vs synthetic; a priori vs a posteriori; necessary vs contingent — the modal/epistemic grid underlies half the exam.
Deontology vs consequentialism vs virtue ethics: know which question each answers (what is my duty? what maximizes good? what would the virtuous person do?).
Compatibilism vs libertarianism vs hard determinism; dualism vs physicalism vs functionalism — position-maps you can draw from memory.
Act vs rule utilitarianism; endurantism vs perdurantism; presentism vs eternalism — the intra-family splits examiners love to probe.

example.code:
The grid (memorize cold):
  EPISTEMIC: a priori (knowable without experience) vs a posteriori
  SEMANTIC: analytic (true by meaning) vs synthetic
  MODAL: necessary (true in all worlds) vs contingent
  ARGUMENT: valid (form) vs sound (form + true premises)
  Cross-cutting: 'analytic a priori necessary' cluster — but each
  distinction is independent. Kant's synthetic a priori breaks the cluster.
example.walkthrough: Distinctions are exam currency: questions are built to punish conflation ('is the argument valid?' answered as 'are the premises true?'). Drill them as pairs until the confusion is impossible.

pitfalls: Learning one side of each pair. The distinction IS the pair — know both.
Treating the grid as trivia. Each cell generates arguments (Kant's whole project is one cell: synthetic a priori).
Conflating the columns: 'a priori' is epistemic, 'necessary' is modal, 'analytic' is semantic.
lessons.try_it: Write each distinction as a pair with a one-line test for telling the sides apart; drill until instant.

lessons.title: Common Question Types Decoded
concepts: 'Is X compatible with Y?' — compatibility questions want a reconciliation or a principled incompatibility proof: show the joint model or derive the contradiction. Do not just describe X and Y.
Thought-experiment prompts ('What does the trolley case show?') want: the setup, the intuition it pumps, what the intuition is evidence FOR, and the standard replies. Four moves, in order.
'Compare A and B' wants a mapped comparison — shared ground, precise difference, verdict on which difference matters — not two mini-essays stapled together.
'Does P entail Q?' is a logic question in disguise: construct the entailment or produce the counterexample model. One counterexample beats ten paragraphs.

example.code:
Decoding 'What does Gettier show?':
  1. SETUP: Smith's coins / the stopped clock — justified true belief by luck.
  2. INTUITION: not knowledge.
  3. EVIDENCE FOR: JTB insufficient; justification must be non-lucky.
  4. REPLIES: no-false-lemmas, reliabilism, virtue epistemology.
  Four moves = full marks. Skip 4 and you cap your grade.
example.walkthrough: Question types are genres with conventions: the examiner has a checklist per type, and the checklist is public knowledge among good students. Learn the four moves for each type and the exam becomes execution, not improvisation.

pitfalls: Answering compatibility questions with descriptions of each side and no verdict.
Narrating the thought experiment without saying what it is evidence for.
Comparing by juxtaposition ('A says... B says...') with no mapping of the difference.
lessons.try_it: Classify your last five practice questions by type and check you used the right four-move structure.

lessons.title: Revision Protocol: The Final Week
concepts: Day 7–5: distinction drills and position maps from memory — rebuild the grids cold, checking against notes only after. What you cannot rebuild, you do not know.
Day 4–3: timed essay outlines (not full essays): 20 minutes per outline on past questions, marked against the skeleton. Outlines train structure; full essays train stamina you already have.
Day 2: the objection ledger review — every confusion you ever logged, re-tested. This is personalized high-yield revision; generic re-reading is low-yield.
Day 1: light review of skeletons and grids only; sleep properly. Cramming new content the night before displaces retrieval of what you know.

example.code:
Final-week calendar:
  D7: distinctions grid, cold rebuild
  D6: position maps (mind, free will, ethics), cold rebuild
  D5: thought-experiment four-movers (Gettier, trolley, Mary, veil)
  D4: 3 timed outlines, marked vs skeleton
  D3: 3 timed outlines, different branches
  D2: objection ledger, full pass
  D1: skeletons + sleep
example.walkthrough: The protocol's principle: test, do not re-read — and test the highest-yield items (distinctions, structures, your own logged confusions) rather than everything equally. Revision is triage.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes cover to cover. Familiarity is not mastery; test instead.
Learning new material on day 1. It interferes with retrieval of the old.
Skipping sleep to cram. Sleep consolidates; the trade is negative.
lessons.try_it: Build your final-week calendar now, working backward from the exam date.

lessons.title: Philosophy — The Branches Map
concepts: Metaphysics asks what is real; epistemology asks what is known and how; ethics asks what is right; logic asks what follows; aesthetics asks what is beautiful. The branches are regions of one territory, not separate subjects.

The branches interlock: your metaphysics constrains your epistemology (what can be known depends on what there is), and your ethics presupposes both (responsibility needs agency, agency needs a metaphysics).
Applied branches inherit the core: philosophy of mind applies metaphysics to thinking; political philosophy applies ethics to institutions; philosophy of science applies epistemology to inquiry.
Exam questions routinely cross branches ('is moral knowledge possible?' = ethics + epistemology). Study the borders, not just the interiors.

example.code:
Branch × question matrix:
  METAPHYSICS: What exists? (universals, causation, time)
  EPISTEMOLOGY: What is knowledge? (JTB, skepticism, testimony)
  ETHICS: What is right? (metaethics, normative, applied)
  LOGIC: What follows? (deduction, induction, fallacies)
  + MIND, POLITICS, SCIENCE, ART as applied regions.
example.walkthrough: The map's value is navigational: when a question mixes branches, you know which toolkits to combine. Most exam failures are branch-mismatches — answering a metaphysical question with epistemological tools.

pitfalls: Treating branches as silos. The interesting questions live at intersections.
Memorizing branch definitions without their questions. Each branch is defined by its central questions.
Skipping 'minor' branches. Aesthetics and philosophy of science appear as wildcards.
lessons.try_it: Draw the branch map from memory, placing three questions in each branch.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Reading Primary Texts
concepts: Read for the argument, not the prose: extract premises, conclusion, and inference into a numbered skeleton before judging. Most primary texts hide their argument in rhetoric.
Track the dialectic: who is the author replying to? Texts are moves in conversations — Hume replies to Locke, Kant replies to Hume. The reply structure is the meaning.
Charity first: reconstruct the strongest version before criticizing. If your reconstruction makes the author look foolish, you have misread — great philosophers are rarely fools.
Read slowly and twice: first pass for the overall move, second pass for premise-level detail. Speed-reading philosophy is an oxymoron.

example.code:
Extraction template:
  TARGET CLAIM: ...
  P1: ...
  P2: ...
  INFERENCE: (modus tollens / abduction / thought experiment...)
  CONCLUSION: ...
  REPLYING TO: (which earlier move?)
  Apply to one page of Descartes' Meditations and watch it clarify.
example.walkthrough: Extraction converts reading from consumption to dissection: you stop asking 'what did he say?' and start asking 'what would break if P2 were false?' That is philosophical reading.

pitfalls: Quoting without reconstructing. A quotation is not an understanding.
Criticizing before charity. The weak version you refute is your own invention.
Reading only summaries. Summaries give conclusions; arguments live in the text.
lessons.try_it: Take one page of a primary text and extract its argument into the template today.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Thought Experiments as Method
concepts: Thought experiments are intuition pumps: controlled scenarios that isolate a variable (the runaway trolley isolates consequences from agency; Mary's room isolates physical facts from experience).

Their evidential role is contested: do intuitions reveal truths about concepts, or just report cultural habits? Experimental philosophy (X-phi) tests whether intuitions vary across demographics — sometimes they do.
The standard critical moves: pump a conflicting intuition (trolley variants), debunk the intuition's source (evolutionary debunking), or deny the case is possible (conceivability doubts).
Exam use: always give setup → intuition → upshot → replies. The thought experiment is evidence in an argument, not a story that speaks for itself.

example.code:
Anatomy of a thought experiment:
  SETUP: stipulated scenario (trolley, veil, Chinese room)
  VARIABLE ISOLATED: what differs from real life, and why
  INTUITION PUMPED: the judgment it elicits
  UPSHOT CLAIMED: the philosophical thesis it supports
  REPLIES: conflicting intuitions, debunking, impossibility charges
example.walkthrough: Seeing the anatomy lets you attack precisely: deny the intuition, deny the upshot follows, or deny the case is coherent. Vague unease is not a reply; targeted moves are.

pitfalls: Treating the intuition as self-evident truth. Intuitions are data, and data can be misleading.
Narrating without upshot. The story is the delivery mechanism, not the point.
Ignoring X-phi. If intuitions vary culturally, their evidential weight needs defense.
lessons.try_it: Take one thought experiment and write all five anatomical parts explicitly.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Philosophy and the Sciences
concepts: Naturalism: philosophy should be continuous with the sciences — no supernatural entities, no a priori access to substantive truths about the world. Most contemporary philosophers are naturalists of some stripe.
The boundary disputes: consciousness (can neuroscience close the explanatory gap?), morality (can evolution debunk moral beliefs?), mathematics (are numbers natural?). Each tests naturalism's limits.

Philosophy of science proper: what distinguishes science (falsifiability? paradigms? research programmes?), what explanation is, and whether science describes reality or saves the phenomena (realism vs anti-realism).
The division of labor: science answers what happens; philosophy clarifies what the answers mean, what they presuppose, and what would count as an answer. Neither replaces the other.

example.code:
The debunking argument (Street), schematized:
  P1: Evolution shaped our moral judgments for fitness, not truth.
  P2: If so, the alignment of our moral beliefs with moral truths
       would be a coincidence.
  C: Our moral beliefs are unjustified (unless we posit a tracking
     explanation).
  Naturalism's own tools turned on morality — the live question is
  whether the tracking explanation exists.
example.walkthrough: Debunking arguments are naturalism's internal critics: they use science's own findings to question regions of belief. Whether they overreach (do they debunk mathematics too?) is the current frontier.

pitfalls: Treating naturalism as scientism ('only science yields knowledge'). Naturalism is continuity, not monopoly.
Assuming philosophy and science compete. They ask different questions about the same world.
Ignoring the boundary cases. Consciousness and morality are where the action is.
lessons.try_it: State one boundary dispute and which side you take, with the cost of your side.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Writing Philosophy
concepts: Clarity is the virtue: short sentences, defined terms, explicit structure. Obscurity is not depth — if you cannot say it plainly, you do not understand it yet.
Signposting: tell the reader where the argument is going ('I will first show X, then argue Y'). Philosophical readers navigate by structure; give them a map.
Definitions do work: define key terms at first use, then use them consistently. Equivocation is the most common student fallacy, and it is always preventable.
Examples earn abstraction: illustrate each abstract claim with a concrete case. The case tests the claim — if no example fits, the claim is empty.

example.code:
Before/after:
  BEFORE: 'The deontological framework's normative force vis-a-vis
  consequentialist aggregation problematizes utility maximization.'
  AFTER: 'Deontology forbids sacrificing one person to save five, even
  when the numbers favor it. Utilitarianism permits it. The dispute is
  whether numbers can override the duty not to use people.'
  Same content; one is checkable.
example.walkthrough: The after-version can be wrong in visible ways — which is exactly why it is better. Checkable prose invites correction; obscure prose hides behind itself. Aim to be refutable.

pitfalls: Mistaking complexity for rigor. Rigor is precision, and precision is usually simple.
Undefined technical terms. Every term of art must earn its introduction.
Example-free abstraction. If you cannot instantiate it, you do not own it.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your last paragraph of philosophical prose: halve the sentence length, define every term.

lessons.title: Philosophy — Key Distinctions Drill
concepts: The modal/epistemic/semantic grid: necessary/contingent (modal), a priori/a posteriori (epistemic), analytic/synthetic (semantic). Kant's synthetic a priori claims one cell of the grid is occupied — the grid organizes centuries of debate.

Internalism vs externalism (epistemology): does justification depend only on what is inside the head (evidence, reasons) or also on external facts (reliability of the process)? Gettier cases fuel externalism.
Cognitivism vs non-cognitivism (metaethics): are moral claims truth-apt beliefs, or expressions of attitude (boo/hurrah)? The disagreement debate is the testing ground.
Type vs token: a type is a kind (the word 'the' as a dictionary entry), a token its instance (each printed 'the'). Identity theory debates trade on this distinction.

example.code:
Drill format (say aloud, 30 seconds each):
  'Validity vs soundness: validity is form — conclusion must follow;
  soundness adds true premises. Test: can a valid argument have a
  false conclusion? Yes — with a false premise.'
  Twelve pairs, daily, until each answer is instant and the test
  case is automatic.
example.walkthrough: Distinctions are tested under time pressure, so drill them under time pressure. The 30-second oral format builds the retrieval speed the exam demands — silent re-reading does not.

pitfalls: Learning definitions without test cases. The test case IS the understanding.
Drilling passively (reading cards). Recall aloud; production, not recognition.
Stopping when 'familiar.' Stop when instant — familiarity is the trap.
lessons.try_it: Run the 12-pair drill aloud today; log every hesitation in the objection ledger.

lessons.title: Augustine: Faith Seeking Understanding
concepts: Evil as privation: evil is not a thing but the absence of good, as blindness is the absence of sight — this dissolves the Manichean picture of warring cosmic powers without denying suffering.
Time as distension of the soul: the past exists as memory, the future as expectation, the present as attention. Time is not 'out there' but in the mind's stretching — a strikingly modern move.
Divine illumination: the mind sees eternal truths (mathematics, logic) by a light from God — an early account of a priori knowledge that makes objectivity theological.
The City of God: history as the interwoven story of two cities — the earthly (love of self) and the heavenly (love of God). Politics is relativized: no earthly regime is ultimate.

example.code:
Against the Manichees:
  'Where does evil come from, if God is good?'
  Augustine's reply: the question assumes evil is a substance.
  A wound is not a thing added to the body but the body's
  goodness damaged. Evil = good deprived of its due measure.
  Corruption presupposes a good thing corrupted.
example.walkthrough: Privation theory does not console the sufferer — it answers the metaphysical question (what IS evil?) so the moral question (why does God permit it?) can be addressed via free will. Keep the two questions distinct.

pitfalls: Reading privation as 'evil isn't real.' It is real as corruption — real the way a hole is real.
Confusing illumination with mysticism. It is an epistemology of necessary truth, not visions.
Missing the political point of the two cities: earthly politics is penultimate, never ultimate.
lessons.try_it: Take one suffering you have witnessed and ask: does privation theory or free-will defense better address it? Why?

lessons.title: Anselm and the Ontological Argument
concepts: The Proslogion argument: God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived.' Even the fool who denies God has this concept in mind — and existing in reality is greater than existing in the mind alone. So God exists in reality.

The argument's audacity: it tries to prove existence from a definition alone — no observation, no cosmology. If it works, reason reaches God a priori; if it fails, the failure teaches the limits of definition.

Gaunilo's reply (On Behalf of the Fool): the same reasoning 'proves' a perfect island — the most excellent island conceivable must exist, else a greater (existing) island is conceivable. Reductio of the form.

Anselm's counter: islands are contingent kinds — 'greatest island' has no intrinsic maximum (always a greater beach). God is not a kind-member but being itself; the reply only works for God. Whether this saves the argument is the live question.

example.code:
The argument, numbered:
  P1: God = that than which nothing greater can be conceived.
  P2: This exists in the understanding (even the fool grasps it).
  P3: Existing in reality is greater than existing in the understanding alone.
  C: Therefore God exists in reality (else something greater —
     the existing God — is conceivable, contradicting P1).
example.walkthrough: The argument turns on P3: is existence a 'greatness-making' property? Kant's famous denial ('existence is not a predicate') targets exactly this premise. Every ontological argument since is a footnote to P3.

pitfalls: Treating Gaunilo as a refutation rather than a challenge. Anselm's reply (kinds vs being-itself) must be answered too.
Thinking 'the fool' means stupid. The fool is the atheist of Psalm 14 — the dialectical opponent.
Assuming the argument is a joke. It convinced serious minds for centuries; condescension is not analysis.
lessons.try_it: Reconstruct Gaunilo's island parody precisely, then state Anselm's best reply in one sentence.

lessons.title: Aquinas: The Five Ways
concepts: The Five Ways (Summa Theologiae I.2.3) are not proofs for believers but demonstrations from observed effects to God as first cause — motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, teleology.

The Third Way (contingency): contingent beings exist (they might not have); if everything were contingent, at some time nothing existed — but nothing comes from nothing; so a necessary being exists, on which all contingency depends.

Natural law: moral principles are the rational creature's participation in eternal law — the first precept, 'good is to be done and evil avoided,' is self-evident to practical reason; specific norms derive from human goods.

Faith and reason as allies: reason can demonstrate God's existence and many moral truths; faith receives what exceeds reason (Trinity, Incarnation). Double-truth is rejected — truth cannot contradict truth.

example.code:
The First Way (motion), compressed:
  1. Some things are in motion (changed).
  2. Whatever is moved is moved by another (nothing moves itself
     from potency to act in the same respect).
  3. No infinite regress of movers (else no first, hence no motion).
  4. Therefore a first unmoved mover exists — 'and this we call God.'
  Note the modesty: the Way proves an unmoved mover, not the Trinity.
example.walkthrough: The Ways' honesty is their scope: each concludes to a metaphysical role (unmoved mover, necessary being, designer), and Aquinas identifies the role with God. Attack either the inference or the identification — critics divide on which.

pitfalls: Reading the Ways as scientific hypotheses. They are metaphysical demonstrations from Aristotelian principles.
Demanding they prove the Christian God. They prove a philosophical God; revelation completes the picture.
Dismissing 'no infinite regress' as arbitrary. It is argued: essentially ordered series need a first member.
lessons.try_it: Formalize the Third Way as numbered premises; identify which premise a Humean would deny.

lessons.title: The Islamic Golden Age: Avicenna and Averroes
concepts: Avicenna's flying man: imagine created suspended in air, senses veiled — he would still affirm his own existence. Self-awareness needs no body: the soul is known directly, proving its distinctness from the body.

The necessary existent: Avicenna's proof distinguishes essence from existence — in contingent things they differ (you can grasp what a phoenix is without it existing); so existence must come from a being whose essence IS existence, the Necessary Existent.

Averroes on faith and reason: philosophy and revelation cannot conflict (truth is one); where scripture seems to contradict demonstration, scripture must be read allegorically — reason judges the interpretation, not the text's authority.

The transmission: without the Islamic philosophers' commentaries and developments, Aristotle would have reached Latin Europe as fragments. Medieval philosophy is unthinkable without Baghdad and Cordoba.

example.code:
Essence vs existence (Avicenna):
  PHOENIX: essence graspable, existence absent -> essence != existence.
  YOU: same — you might not have existed.
  Therefore every contingent thing receives existence from another.
  Regress impossible -> a being whose essence IS existence:
  the Necessary Existent, existing through itself.
example.walkthrough: The essence/existence distinction became the engine of Latin metaphysics (Aquinas's real distinction). Avicenna's proof moves by conceptual analysis where Aquinas's Ways move by cosmology — two routes to the necessary being, worth comparing premise by premise.

pitfalls: Treating Islamic philosophy as mere transmission. Avicenna and Averroes are original metaphysicians, not couriers.
Reading the flying man as mysticism. It is an epistemological argument about self-knowledge.
Missing Averroes' boldness: reason gets the last word on interpretation — within a faithful framework.
lessons.try_it: Compare Avicenna's necessary existent with Aquinas's Third Way: which premise does each depend on?

lessons.title: Ockham and the End of Scholasticism
concepts: Ockham's razor: 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' — do not posit more than the explanation requires. A methodological principle, not a metaphysical one: simpler theories are preferable, ceteris paribus.
Nominalism about universals: only particulars exist; 'humanity' is a name (nomen) for resembling individuals, not a shared entity. This dismantles much of scholastic realism in one move.

Divine command and contingency: God's will is radically free — morality depends on divine command, and the created order could have been otherwise. This voluntarism unsettles the confident rationalism of Aquinas.
Why Ockham matters: razor + nominalism + emphasis on logic over metaphysics prefigures empiricism and modern science. The medieval synthesis ends not with refutation but with a new toolkit.

example.code:
Applying the razor:
  SCHOLASTIC: universals exist as real entities explaining resemblance.
  OCKHAM: resembling particulars + the mind's concept suffice.
  Verdict: the universal-entity explains nothing the concept doesn't —
  shave it off. The explanation must earn its ontology.
example.walkthrough: The razor's discipline is ontological honesty: every entity in your theory must do explanatory work. Theories accumulate entities like code accumulates dependencies — the razor is refactoring for metaphysics.

pitfalls: Treating the razor as 'the simplest answer is true.' It is a preference rule for theory choice, not a truth detector.
Reading nominalism as denying similarity. Resemblance is real; shared universal-entities are what is denied.
Thinking Ockham was anti-religious. His fideism protects faith from philosophy's overreach — a theological motive.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your own beliefs and apply the razor: which entities in it do no explanatory work?

lessons.title: Descartes: Methodic Doubt
concepts: Methodic doubt: reject every belief that can be doubted — senses deceive, dreams mimic waking, an evil demon could fake everything. The point is not skepticism but foundations: find what survives.
The cogito: 'I think, therefore I am' — doubting itself proves the doubter exists. It survives the demon because deception presupposes someone deceived. The one indubitable starting point.
The wax argument: a wax's sensible properties all change near fire, yet we judge it the same wax — so identity is grasped by intellect, not senses. The mind is better known than the body.

The Cartesian circle worry: Descartes proves God (non-deceiver) via clear and distinct ideas, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. Whether the circle is vicious is a four-century debate.

example.code:
The doubt ladder:
  1. Senses sometimes deceive -> don't fully trust them.
  2. Dreaming mimics waking -> can't prove you're awake.
  3. Evil demon fakes everything -> even mathematics?
  SURVIVOR: the doubting self. 'Deceive me all you like —
  there must be an I to be deceived.'
example.walkthrough: The Meditations are a six-day exercise, not a treatise: each day's doubt clears ground for the next day's rebuilding. Read them as spiritual exercises in epistemology and the structure clicks.

pitfalls: Treating the cogito as a syllogism ('all thinkers exist...'). It is a direct intuition, not an inference.
Thinking Descartes stayed a skeptic. The doubt is methodological — a demolition phase before reconstruction.
Missing the wax argument's point: it proves the intellect's priority, setting up mind-body dualism.
lessons.try_it: Run the doubt ladder on one of your beliefs; note exactly where it stops.

lessons.title: Rationalists: Spinoza and Leibniz
concepts: Spinoza's monism: there is one substance — God-or-Nature (Deus sive Natura) — with infinite attributes, of which we know two (thought, extension). Minds and bodies are modes of the one substance, not separate things.
The payoff: no interaction problem (no two substances to interact), and freedom redefined — free is what follows from one's own nature alone. Humans are free when acting from adequate ideas.

Leibniz's monads: reality is infinitely many simple, windowless substances (monads), each mirroring the universe from its viewpoint, coordinated by pre-established harmony — no causal interaction, perfect synchronization.

The Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR): nothing is without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise. Leibniz's master key — it drives the cosmological argument, optimism ('best of all possible worlds'), and much else.

example.code:
Spinoza's substance argument (Ethics I):
  1. Substance is what is in itself and conceived through itself.
  2. Two substances sharing an attribute would be indistinguishable.
  3. God has all attributes (has the most reality).
  4. So no substance besides God is possible.
  C: One substance; you and I are its modes (like waves of the sea).
example.walkthrough: Spinoza's definitions do the heavy lifting — the Ethics is geometry-style, so every fight is about the definitions. If 'substance' means what he says, monism follows; deny the definition and the system never starts. Learn to attack definitions.

pitfalls: Reading Spinoza as an atheist pamphleteer. 'God-or-Nature' is pantheism with logical rigor, not provocation.
Treating monads as tiny physical atoms. They are metaphysical simples — soul-like, non-spatial.
Missing PSR's scope: Leibniz applies it to everything, including God's choices — which generates the determinism debates.
lessons.try_it: State Spinoza's definition of substance in your own words; then say what follows if you reject it.

lessons.title: Empiricists: Locke, Berkeley, Hume
concepts: Locke's tabula rasa: the mind begins blank; all ideas come from sensation and reflection. Against innate ideas: if principles were innate, children and 'idiots' would know them — they do not.

Locke on personal identity: the person goes with consciousness/memory, not the body (the prince and the cobbler). Identity is forensic — it grounds responsibility, so it tracks what we can own as ours.
Berkeley's immaterialism: esse est percipi — to be is to be perceived. Matter is an empty abstraction; reality is minds and their ideas, sustained by God's perception when we are not looking.

Hume's fork and skepticism: relations of ideas (math, certain) vs matters of fact (causal, never certain). Causation is constant conjunction plus mental habit; induction has no rational justification — custom, not reason, runs our lives.

example.code:
Hume on causation (Enquiry):
  1. We observe A followed by B, repeatedly. (constant conjunction)
  2. We never observe any 'necessary connection' between them.
  3. The expectation that B will follow A is habit/custom.
  C: Causal necessity is a projection of the mind, not a perception.
  Upshot: science's core concept rests on feeling, not reason.
example.walkthrough: Hume is the great solvent: apply his fork to any grand claim and watch it dissolve into 'relations of ideas' (prove it) or 'matters of fact' (show the impression). Kant said Hume woke him from 'dogmatic slumber' — the next lesson is the alarm's result.

pitfalls: Reading Berkeley as denying tables exist. He denies mind-independent matter, not tables — tables are stable ideas.
Thinking Hume denied causation. He denied we perceive necessity; constant conjunction plus habit is his account.
Missing Locke's political Locke: the same book grounds property and revolution. Epistemology had politics.
lessons.try_it: Apply Hume's fork to one of your strong beliefs: which side does it fall on, and what follows?

lessons.title: Kant: The Copernican Turn
concepts: The Copernican turn: objects conform to our cognition, not cognition to objects. Space, time, and the categories (causality, substance) are forms our minds impose — we know phenomena (things-as-they-appear), never noumena (things-in-themselves).

The synthetic a priori: mathematics and the basic principles of science are informative (synthetic) yet knowable without experience (a priori) — because they articulate the mind's own forms. Hume's skepticism answered: necessity comes from us.

The categorical imperative: act only on maxims you can will as universal law; treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Morality's authority is reason's self-legislation — autonomy, not divine command or utility.

The antinomies: reason overreaches when it treats the world-whole as an object — proving both that the world has a beginning and that it does not. The contradictions diagnose reason's limits, licensing the phenomena/noumena split.

example.code:
The categorical imperative, three formulations (one law):
  1. UNIVERSAL LAW: act only on maxims you could will as universal.
     (Can 'lie when convenient' be universalized? No — trust collapses.)
  2. HUMANITY: never treat persons merely as means.
  3. KINGDOM OF ENDS: act as legislating member of a moral community.
  Test a maxim: universalize it; if it self-destructs, it's forbidden.
example.walkthrough: Kant's system is architectonic: the first Critique limits knowledge to make room for faith (and freedom); the second grounds morality in autonomy; the third bridges nature and freedom via beauty and purpose. Each Critique answers the previous one's opening.

pitfalls: Reading 'Copernican turn' as subjectivism. The forms are universal and necessary — objectivity reconstructed, not abandoned.
Treating noumena as a second world. It is a limiting concept: what lies beyond our forms, not a place.
Applying the imperative as a decision procedure for everything. It tests maxims; judgment still does work.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your maxims ('cut corners when unobserved') and run the universalization test.

lessons.title: After Kant: Hegel to Nietzsche
concepts: Hegel's dialectic: reality is the unfolding of Geist (spirit/mind) through contradiction — thesis, antithesis, synthesis (Aufhebung: cancel, preserve, lift up). History is reason becoming conscious of itself as freedom.

Master-slave dialectic: self-consciousness needs recognition; the master depends on the slave's recognition, the slave through labor transforms the world — dependence inverts. Recognition is the social core of the self.

Nietzsche's hammer: 'God is dead' — the Christian-Platonic value system has collapsed under its own honesty; nihilism is the danger, and the response is revaluation: create values from strength, not resentment.

Will to power and perspectivism: life is will to power (growth, overcoming); there are no facts, only interpretations — but some perspectives are healthier (life-affirming) than others. Perspectivism is not 'anything goes.'

example.code:
Master-slave, compressed:
  Two consciousnesses meet; each demands recognition.
  Fight -> one submits (slave), one dominates (master).
  Master: recognized by one he doesn't recognize -> hollow.
  Slave: through labor, shapes the world -> finds independence.
  Upshot: domination is self-undermining; recognition must be mutual.
example.walkthrough: The dialectic's lesson for argument: do not refute the opponent — sublate them. Show how their truth is preserved at a higher level that also resolves its contradiction. It is steelmanning as metaphysics.

pitfalls: Reading dialectic as 'thesis-antithesis-synthesis' formula. Hegel never used the triad; it is a textbook simplification.
Treating Nietzsche as a nihilist. He diagnoses nihilism to overcome it — the revaluation is the project.
Taking 'no facts, only interpretations' as relativism. Nietzsche ranks perspectives: health vs sickness.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your beliefs and ask Nietzsche's question: does it spring from strength or resentment?

lessons.title: Metaethics: What Are Moral Claims?
concepts: Cognitivism: moral claims express beliefs, true or false ('stealing is wrong' states a fact). Non-cognitivism: they express attitudes — 'boo stealing!' (emotivism) or prescriptions ('don't steal!' — prescriptivism).

Moral realism vs anti-realism: are there mind-independent moral facts? Realists (naturalist or non-naturalist like Moore) say yes; error theorists (Mackie) say our moral talk presupposes facts that do not exist — so all moral claims are false.

Relativism: moral truth varies by culture or individual. The classic objection: it makes moral disagreement impossible (we just talk past each other) and reformers (abolitionists) into the mistaken ones.
The is-ought gap (Hume): no description of how things are entails how they ought to be without a bridging moral premise. Every moral argument must smuggle or state its 'ought' — find it.

example.code:
Mackie's queerness argument:
  P1: If moral facts existed, they'd be utterly unlike anything
       else — objectively prescriptive (telling us what to do just
       by being true).
  P2: Such 'queer' entities are metaphysically suspect.
  C: Probably no moral facts exist (error theory).
  Realist reply: the queerness is the point — normativity is
  sui generis, not reducible. Standoff? Or decisive?
example.walkthrough: Metaethics is the exam's trapdoor: students argue trolley cases while the question asks whether 'wrong' even refers. Always check which level the question targets — first-order (what is right?) or meta (what are we doing when we say 'right'?).

pitfalls: Treating relativism as tolerance. Relativism is a semantic thesis; tolerance is a moral one — they are independent.
Assuming error theory means 'anything goes.' The error theorist can still condemn — as attitude, not fact.
Missing the is-ought gap in policy arguments. 'Data shows X' never entails 'do X' alone.
lessons.try_it: Take one moral claim you endorse and classify it: cognitivist or not? realist or not?

lessons.title: Utilitarianism: The Greatest Happiness
concepts: Act utilitarianism (Bentham): judge each act by its consequences — maximize total happiness (pleasure minus pain). The felicific calculus tried to quantify: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity.
Mill's refinement: higher pleasures (intellectual, aesthetic) outweigh lower ones — 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' Competent judges who have known both prefer the higher.

Rule utilitarianism: follow the rules whose general observance maximizes happiness ('don't lie') — capturing commonsense constraints while keeping consequences primary. Collapses into act-utilitarianism? The classic worry.

Standard objections: demandingness (must you give away everything?), justice (sacrificing the innocent for the many), prediction (we cannot compute consequences). Each has a utilitarian reply — learn both sides.

example.code:
The transplant case:
  A surgeon can kill one healthy patient and save five with organs.
  Act-utilitarianism seems to permit — even require — it.
  Replies: (1) rule-utilitarianism forbids (the rule destroys trust);
  (2) long-run consequences (no one visits hospitals);
  (3) bite the bullet (yes, do it — our horror is bias).
  Which reply costs most?
example.walkthrough: The transplant case is utilitarianism's crucible: every reply reveals a commitment. (1) and (2) keep the theory commonsensical at the cost of looking ad hoc; (3) keeps it principled at the cost of monstrousness. There is no free reply — that is the lesson.

pitfalls: Treating utilitarianism as selfishness. It is impartial — your happiness counts once, no more.
Confusing act and rule versions. The transplant divides them precisely.
Assuming consequences means 'short-term.' Utilitarians count ALL consequences — the theory is demanding, not myopic.
lessons.try_it: Run the transplant case against all three utilitarian replies; rank them by cost.

lessons.title: Deontology: Duty and the Categorical Imperative
concepts: Kant's project: morality's authority comes from reason's self-legislation (autonomy), not from God, consequences, or inclination. A good will — acting from duty — is the only unconditional good.
Universal law formulation: act only on maxims you can will as universal law. Lying fails: universalized lying destroys the trust lying exploits — a practical contradiction.
Humanity formulation: treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Persons have dignity (unconditional worth), not price — this grounds rights against aggregation.

Contemporary deontology: Ross's prima facie duties (fidelity, beneficence, non-maleficence...) — plural, weighable, commonsensical; and contractualism (Scanlon): principles no one could reasonably reject.

example.code:
The murderer at the door (Kant's hard case):
  A murderer asks where your friend hides. Kant says: do not lie —
  even here. Critics: this is monstrous rigorism.
  Kant's reply: you are responsible for your maxim, not the
  consequences; lying corrupts the shared condition of truth.
  Modern Kantians (Korsgaard): the duty is to the murderer as
  rational agent too — but may we refuse to answer? The debate continues.
example.walkthrough: The murderer case tests whether deontology is principle or fanaticism. Kant's defenders distinguish lying from misleading silence; his critics say any theory that forbids lying to murderers has refuted itself. Know both — the exam loves this case.

pitfalls: Reading Kant as 'follow rules blindly.' The rules are self-legislated by reason — autonomy, not obedience.
Treating the formulations as separate theories. They are one law, three expressions.
Assuming deontology ignores consequences. It denies they determine rightness, not that they matter.
lessons.try_it: Formulate one of your maxims; test it against both the universal-law and humanity formulations.

lessons.title: Virtue Ethics: Character First
concepts: Aristotle's starting point: ethics asks 'how should one live?' not 'what should I do?' — eudaimonia (flourishing) is the goal, virtues are the stable character traits that constitute it.

Virtues as means: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and waste — found by phronesis (practical wisdom), not by formula. The mean is relative to the person and situation.
The unity question: can you be courageous but unjust? Aristotle suggests the virtues hang together via phronesis; contemporary virtue ethicists debate how tight the unity is.

Modern revival (Anscombe, Foot, MacIntyre): 'modern moral philosophy' is broken — 'ought' without a divine lawgiver is incoherent; return to virtue concepts (just, courageous, temperate) grounded in human flourishing.

example.code:
Phronesis vs rules:
  RULE: 'Always tell the truth.'
  CASE: Your friend's terrible haircut, beaming, asks your opinion.
  The rule-follower blurts cruelty or lies.
  The phronimos discerns: honesty without cruelty — 'it's bold;
  the color suits you' — truthful, kind, context-sensitive.
  Virtue is skill, not algorithm.
example.walkthrough: Virtue ethics' distinctive claim: right action is what the virtuous person would do — character is explanatorily prior to rules. Critics call this circular (how do we identify the virtuous?); defenders say moral learning is apprenticeship, like craft.

pitfalls: Treating virtue ethics as 'be a good person' vagueness. The virtues are specific, the mean is determinate-ish, phronesis is a skill.
Assuming it cannot guide action. 'What would the virtuous person do?' is action-guiding via exemplars.
Missing Anscombe's radicalism: she thinks 'morally ought' is a leftover concept — the revival starts from conceptual bankruptcy.
lessons.try_it: Identify one virtue you lack; describe its excess, deficiency, and what phronesis would look like in your life.

lessons.title: Applied Ethics: Hard Cases
concepts: The trolley problem (Foot, Thomson): diverting the trolley (5 vs 1) seems permissible; pushing the large person seems wrong — same numbers, different verdict. What explains the difference? Doctrine of double effect? Agent-centered constraints?

Animals: Singer's sentience criterion — if suffering matters, species membership is arbitrary (speciesism). Regan's rights view: animals are subjects-of-a-life with inherent value. The practical upshot is dietary and experimental.

Future people: our actions shape unborn generations (climate, AI). Parfit's non-identity problem: if our choice determines WHO exists, can we harm them? Person-affecting vs impersonal ethics divides the field.
Tech ethics: algorithmic bias (whose values in the loss function?), autonomous weapons (who decides to kill?), AI alignment (whose morality gets encoded?). Applied ethics is now engineering ethics.

example.code:
The non-identity problem (Parfit):
  Policy A: conservation -> future people live well.
  Policy B: depletion -> different future people live less well.
  B's people wouldn't exist under A — so did B harm them?
  They can't say 'you made ME worse off' (no alternative THEM).
  Yet B seems wrong. Person-affecting principles break here;
  impersonal principles ('make the world better') survive.
example.walkthrough: Applied ethics' method: take a principle, run it against cases, revise. The cases are not puzzles for fun — each isolates a feature (agency, identity, numbers) that principles must handle. Master the cases and you master the principles' costs.

pitfalls: Treating intuitions as verdicts. Intuitions are data; principles explain them — and data can mislead.
Solving trolley by picking a side. The question is what EXPLAINS the verdict-difference.
Ignoring the non-identity problem's depth. It threatens all person-affecting ethics — including commonsense.
lessons.try_it: Take one tech-ethics issue and run it through all three normative frameworks; compare verdicts.

lessons.title: The JTB Analysis and Gettier
concepts: The tripartite analysis: S knows P iff (1) P is true, (2) S believes P, (3) S is justified in believing P. Each condition is necessary; together, supposedly sufficient. Elegant — and, Gettier showed, wrong.

Gettier's counterexamples (1963): Smith believes 'the man with ten coins will get the job' — justified (the boss said so, Smith counted coins), true (Smith himself gets the job, and has ten coins) — but Smith does not KNOW. Justified true belief by luck.
The diagnosis: justification can be accidentally connected to truth — the belief is true for reasons unrelated to the justification. Knowledge requires a non-accidental connection.

Responses: add a 'no false lemmas' condition; require causal connection (Goldman); require the truth to be creditable to the agent's competence (virtue epistemology, Sosa); or go externalist (reliabilism).

example.code:
Gettier's Smith case, step by step:
  EVIDENCE: boss says Jones gets the job; Smith counted 10 coins
            in Jones's pocket.
  BELIEF: 'The man with 10 coins will get the job.' (justified)
  TWIST: Smith gets the job; unknown to all, Smith has 10 coins.
  STATUS: true + believed + justified — but LUCKY. Not knowledge.
  The justification pointed at Jones; the truth came via Smith.
example.walkthrough: Gettier's paper is three pages and ended a 2,400-year consensus — the best argument-to-length ratio in philosophy. Its lesson for method: conceptual analysis is hostage to counterexamples, and one clean case beats volumes of theory.

pitfalls: Thinking Gettier refutes 'justified' or 'true belief.' He grants all three conditions and denies sufficiency.
Requiring certainty as the fix. Knowledge does not need certainty — it needs non-lucky justification.
Missing the generality: every JTB+ patch faces new Gettier-style cases (the 'Gettier industry').
lessons.try_it: Construct your own Gettier case in a tech setting (a dashboard, a log, a metric).

lessons.title: Skepticism: Brains, Dreams, and Demons
concepts: Cartesian skepticism: for any belief about the external world, a skeptical scenario (dream, demon, brain in a vat) is indistinguishable from reality — so you cannot know you are not in it, and (by closure) cannot know the world exists.

The closure principle: if you know P, and know P entails Q, then you know Q. The skeptic's engine: you know 'I have hands' entails 'I am not a handless brain in a vat'; you do not know the latter; so you do not know the former.

Humean skepticism about induction: no rational justification for expecting the future to resemble the past — the uniformity principle itself needs induction (circular) or deduction (impossible). Custom, not reason.

Replies: deny closure (Dretske, Nozick — but at what cost?), contextualism ('knows' means different things in different contexts), or Mooreanism ('here is one hand' — commonsense as evidence against the skeptic's premises).

example.code:
The skeptic's argument from ignorance:
  P1: You don't know you're not a brain in a vat. (indistinguishable)
  P2: If you don't know that, you don't know you have hands. (closure:
      'I have hands' entails 'I'm not a handless vat-brain')
  C: You don't know you have hands.
  Every reply denies a premise. Which would you deny — and what
  does denying it cost?
example.walkthrough: Skeptical arguments are valuable even if unsound: they map the exact price of our knowledge claims. Each reply to skepticism IS a theory of knowledge — contextualism, reliabilism, and Mooreanism all started as anti-skeptical moves.

pitfalls: Treating skepticism as a mood. It is a set of arguments with premises to deny — do the work.
Assuming the skeptic must be answered. Some accept the conclusion for ordinary standards (fallibilism).
Confusing 'cannot refute the skeptic' with 'skepticism is true.' Undefeated is not victorious.
lessons.try_it: Pick one skeptical argument and state its premises; choose your denial and price it.

lessons.title: Rationalism vs Empiricism
concepts: Rationalism: some substantive knowledge comes from reason alone — innate ideas or a priori insight (mathematics, metaphysics). Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz: the senses are secondary; reason is the organ of truth.

Empiricism: all substantive knowledge comes from experience — the mind is a tabula rasa (Locke); even apparently a priori truths are habits or definitions (Hume). Test every claim against the impressions.

The innate-ideas debate: Leibniz's reply to Locke — the mind is not a blank tablet but veined marble; experience reveals the veins. Nativism returns in Chomsky (universal grammar) and cognitive science.

Kant's synthesis: empiricism is right that knowledge begins with experience; rationalism is right that not all of it arises from experience — the mind contributes forms (space, time, categories). The debate's Aufhebung.

example.code:
Locke vs Leibniz on the mind:
  LOCKE: blank tablet; experience writes everything.
  LEIBNIZ: veined marble; the veins (innate structure) shape
           what experience reveals.
  MODERN ECHO: Chomsky's poverty of the stimulus — children learn
  language from too little data; something innate must help.
  The debate never died; it moved into cognitive science.
example.walkthrough: The rationalism/empiricism divide is really about the mind's contribution: is the mind a mirror (empiricism) or a lamp (rationalism)? Kant's answer — both, in different respects — remains the most influential settlement.

pitfalls: Treating the debate as historical. Nativism vs empiricism is live in linguistics, vision science, and AI.
Reading 'innate' as 'conscious at birth.' Innate means structurally present, not explicitly known.
Assuming Kant ended the debate. He reframed it; the frame is still contested.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your skills (debugging? language?) and ask: what in it could NOT come from experience alone?

lessons.title: Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology
concepts: Process reliabilism (Goldman): a belief is justified iff produced by a reliable process — one that tends to produce true beliefs. Justification becomes an external matter: the process's track record, not the agent's introspection.

The new-evil-demon problem: a demon-victim with identical experiences but systematically false beliefs seems justified — yet her processes are unreliable. Internalist intuitions die hard; reliabilists reply by relativizing reliability to normal worlds.

Virtue epistemology (Sosa): knowledge is apt belief — accurate because adroit. The archer analogy: a shot is apt when it hits the target BECAUSE of skill, not luck. Gettier cases are inapt: true, but not because of competence.
The value problem: why is knowledge more valuable than mere true belief? Sosa's answer: aptness adds credit — knowledge is an achievement, and achievements have distinctive value.

example.code:
Sosa's AAA structure:
  ACCURATE: the belief is true (hits the target).
  ADROIT: it manifests epistemic competence (skill, not flail).
  APT: accurate BECAUSE adroit (the skill explains the hit).
  Gettier's Smith: accurate (true) + adroit (good evidence-use)
  but NOT apt — the truth came via luck, not competence.
example.walkthrough: Virtue epistemology reframes Gettier: the problem was never justification's strength but its connection to truth. 'Because of competence' is doing the work that JTB+ patches kept missing — which is why Sosa's framework absorbed the Gettier industry.

pitfalls: Reading reliabilism as 'whatever works.' Reliability is a precise external condition with counterexamples (demon, clairvoyance).
Missing the demon problem's force: it shows internalist intuitions survive externalist theories — the debate's fault line.
Treating 'virtue' as moral. Epistemic virtues are truth-directed competences, not kindness.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your true beliefs and ask Sosa's question: is it true BECAUSE of your competence?

lessons.title: Testimony and Disagreement
concepts: Testimony is our main knowledge source — science, news, history all run on it. Reductionism (Hume): testimony needs independent backing; non-reductionism (Reid, Burge): we are entitled to trust unless we have defeaters.

The problem of peer disagreement: an equally informed, equally rational peer disagrees with you. Conciliationism: lower your confidence (split the difference). Steadfastness: hold your ground — your evidence includes your reasoning.
The stakes: conciliationism seems to demand skepticism about philosophy, politics, religion — anywhere peers disagree. If you conciliate everywhere, little survives; if nowhere, you are dogmatic.

Expertise and trust: real disagreement is rarely peer-to-peer — credentials, track records, and incentives differ. Social epistemology studies the division of cognitive labor: whom to trust is itself an epistemic skill.

example.code:
The restaurant check (peer disagreement, simplified):
  You and a friend, both good at mental math, split a bill.
  You get $43; she gets $45. Same evidence, equal reliability.
  Conciliationist: suspend or split — your $43 is now shaky.
  Steadfast: trust your calculation; you did the work.
  Which is rational? Now scale up to philosophy, politics, God.
example.walkthrough: Disagreement epistemology matters practically: it governs how you update on expert dissent, code-review disputes, and panel decisions. The restaurant case is the lab; the scaling-up is the exam — and the life skill.
